DECISION 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
SUMMARY 
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority or PURA) approves an annual 
revenue requirement for Yankee Gas Services Company d/b/a Eversource Energy 
(Yankee or Company) in the amount of $802,243,646 for the rate year, November 1, 2025 
– October 31, 2026 (Rate Year).  Notably, reflected in this amount is the Company’s refund 
of a total of $40,218,430 in ratepayer money over the next three years.  The revenue 
requirement includes an allowed return on equity (ROE) of 9.48%; however, the Authority 
reduces the allowed ROE by an aggregate 16 basis points, i.e., to 9.32%, to address 
certain management and compliance issues. 
The Authority declines to approve a multi-year, “performance-based” rate plan 
(MYPB rate plan) that would increase rates each year over a four-year period. 
The Company proposed a 26.80%, or $192,955,454 increase, over currently 
authorized revenues of $719,998,000—the largest requested rate increase by a 
Connecticut gas company in the last 20 yearsF—for a total revenue requirement of 
$912,953,454.1  The Company also proposed a 10.30% ROE—a 100 basis point increase 
from the currently allowed ROE of 9.30%—plus a 50 basis point regulatory risk premium. 
Importantly, the Company has not had a fully adjudicated rate case since 2011.  Its 
2017 rate amendment application was resolved through a settlement agreement (18-05-
10 Agreement).  Under the terms of the 18-05-10 Agreement, the Company continued to 
earn healthy returns.  In 2024, the Authority notified the Company that it would be subject 
to a financial audit unless it filed a rate amendment application.  This application followed. 
B. 
BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING 
Yankee is a public service company within the meaning of General Statutes § 16-
1.  Yankee is an operating subsidiary of Eversource Energy (Eversource or EESCO).  
Application, p. 9.  The Company currently provides gas service to over 252,300 
residential, commercial, and industrial customers in 85 towns and cities in Connecticut.  
Id. 
Yankee previously increased its base distribution rates in 2018.  Decision, Dec. 12, 
2018, Docket No. 18-05-10, Application of Yankee Gas Services Company d/b/a 
Eversource Energy to Increase Its Rates and Charges (18-05-10 Decision). 
On July 22, 2024, the Authority notified the Company that, pursuant to General 
Statutes § 16-19a(a), the Authority would conduct a financial audit of the Company unless 
the Company filed a rate amendment application.  PURA Corresp., July 22, 2024.  On

The Authority conducted a noticed revenue audit of the Company on January 7, 
2025, via remote access, and noticed audits of the books and records of the Company

E. 
POSITION OF THE PARTIES AND INTERVENORS 
The Company seeks to amend its rates to increase its authorized revenues by 
approximately $209 million effective November 1, 2025.  Application, p. 2.  Yankee’s 
proposed rate increase would result in the average residential heating customer 
experiencing a total annual bill impact of 43% or $46.74 monthly increase and the impact 
on commercial and industrial customers would range from a 14% to 42% increase.  Id., 
p. 3.  Yankee states that the increase is necessary to address a distribution operating 
deficiency identified as the difference between the Company’s operating and investment 
costs compared to total revenues Yankee has generated through the rate year.  Id., p. 2.  
The Company attributes the operating deficiency to system and infrastructure 
investments; operating and maintenance expenses; increased proposed depreciation 
rates; and recovery of regulatory assets, such as hardship uncollectible expense.  Id., p. 
3.  Subsequently, Yankee revised its proposed revenue increase to $192,955,522 during 
the proceeding.  Late Filed Ex. 1-SP03, Ex. YGS-REVREQ-2-A, B, C, D Schedules (Ex. 
2), Sch. A-1.0, p. 2.  On October 23, 2025, the Company submitted Motion No. 134

OCC actively participated in this proceeding, issuing hundreds of interrogatories, 
providing expert testimony, conducting cross examination during the evidentiary and late 
filed hearings, and by filing a brief.  OCC cites several concerns with Yankee’s rate 
amendment application, the first being OCC’s recommendation that the Authority to 
exclude unsupported or imprudent plant additions from rate base.  OCC Brief, p. 8.  
Further, OCC suggests the Authority reject the Company’s proposed overall rate of return 
of 7.88% and cost of equity of 10.30% and instead adopt the analysis of OCC’s witness, 
Dr. Woolridge, which suggests a ROE of no higher than 9.38%, for a total maximum rate 
of return on rate base of 7.04%.  Id.  OCC opposes Yankee’s proposed net salvage

Id.  Also, OCC recommends the Authority disallow several expenses, such as incentive 
compensation that benefits shareholders at ratepayer expense, “lush and extraneous 
employee perks” paid for by ratepayers, and other internal costs and unverified 
environmental remediation expenses.  Id., pp. 8–9.  Additionally, OCC disagrees with 
Yankee’s classification of customer complaints and its digital engagement performance 
incentives.  Id., p. 9.  It also notes that Yankee’s current Clean Technology activities are 
not serving the interests of its ratepayers.  Id.  OCC also opposes the Company’s 
proposed MYPB and Performance Incentive Mechanisms; however, OCC supports 
Yankee’s proposed metrics and scorecards but raises concerns with their proposed 
structures.  Id.  Lastly, OCC supports the implementation of a low-income discount rate 
but recommends a different approach to Yankee’s proposed rate design.  Id.

CLF participated in this proceeding, issuing 11 interrogatories, conducting cross

Authority direct Yankee to modify its long-term planning and capital investments in order

stakeholder engagement, CLF recommends the Authority establish a statewide “future of

II. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW 
The Authority is statutorily charged with regulating the rates of Connecticut’s public 
service companies.  General Statutes § 16-19.  The term “public service company” is 
defined to include gas companies, such as Yankee.  See General Statutes § 16-1.  
Consequently, Yankee must “file any proposed amendment of its existing rates with the 
[A]uthority in such form and in accordance with such reasonable regulations as the 
[A]uthority may prescribe.”11  General Statutes § 16-19(a).  Once a proposed rate 
amendment has been filed, the Authority is responsible for making “such investigation of 
such proposed amendment of rates as is necessary to determine whether such rates 
conform to the principles and guidelines” in General Statutes § 16-19e, and the Authority 
must investigate whether the rates “are unreasonably discriminatory or more or less than 
just, reasonable and adequate, or that the service furnished by such company is 
inadequate to or in excess of public necessity and convenience . . . .”  General Statutes 
§ 16-19(a). 
Importantly, a public service company bears “the burden of proving the proposed 
rate under consideration is just and reasonable.”  General Statutes § 16-22.  In placing 
the burden on the company in rate cases, the General Assembly has attempted to remedy 
a critical challenge in setting rates—asymmetric access to information.  The utility 
maintains most of the relevant and critical information necessary for the Authority to make 
findings of fact and associated determinations on rates.  Therefore, the Authority and 
other parties are at an information disadvantage compared to the utility and must rely on 
the utility’s application materials, the utility’s responses to interrogatories, and the utility’s 
witness testimony.  Accordingly, the burden of proof established by General Statutes § 
 
11Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-1-53 et seq. apply to rate amendment applications.

16-22 addresses the information imbalance by imposing an affirmative obligation on the 
utility to present sufficient evidence to support its proposed rate amendment. 
In administrative proceedings, which are subject to the provisions of the Uniform 
Administrative Procedures Act (UAPA), General Statutes § 4-166 et seq., the appropriate 
standard of proof is the preponderance of the evidence.  See Jones v. Connecticut 
Medical Examining Board, 309 Conn. 727, 734–35, 741 n.7 (2013) (“default rule is the 
preponderance of the evidence standard in the absence of legislation to the contrary”); 
Goldstar Medical Services, Inc. v. Dept. of Social Services, 288 Conn. 790, 821 (2008) 
(same).  “That burden of proof is met when [the company] shows the facts supporting [its] 
case are found to be more probable than not.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. 
Connecticut Dept. of Public Utility Control, No. CV094019951S, 2010 WL 797137, at *10 
(Conn. Super. Ct. Feb. 5, 2010) (citing Tianti v. William Raveis Real Estate, Inc., 231 
Conn. 690, 702 (1995)).  Consequently, to carry its statutory burden, the utility must 
provide (or ensure the record contains) evidence that, inter alia, the requested rates are 
consistent with the principles that rates be “sufficient, but no more than sufficient,” General 
Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4), and “reflect prudent and efficient management.”  General 
Statutes § 16-19e(a)(5). 
Notably, the utility bears the burden of providing more than mere declarations of 
fact.  Connecticut Natural Gas Corp. v. Public Utilities Commission, 29 Conn. Supp. 379, 
394 (1971) (finding “no sacrosanctity about the testimony of any company officer 
regardless of his position which gives such testimony any godlike fiat that must be 
accepted out of hand” by the Authority).  “Bald statements need to be covered with some 
evidential hair” before they are acceptable.  Id.  Further, “[a]n administrative agency is not 
required to believe any witness, even an expert.”  Goldstar, 288 Conn. at 830.  It is the 
province of the trier of fact, in this case, the Authority, to “make determinations of 
credibility, crediting some, all, or none of a given witness’ testimony.”  Id. 
The Authority’s review of the proposed rates is guided, in part, by the principle “that 
the level and structure of rates be sufficient, but no more than sufficient, to allow public 
service companies to cover their operating and capital costs, to attract needed capital 
and to maintain their financial integrity, and yet provide appropriate protection to the 
relevant public interests, both existing and foreseeable.”  General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4).  
That language “tracks, almost verbatim, the language that the United States Supreme 
Court used in Hope when it interpreted the ‘just and reasonable’ requirement under the 
Natural Gas Act and the federal constitution.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. Dept. of 
Public Utility Control, 216 Conn. 627, 635 (1990) (referencing Federal Power Commission 
v. Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U.S. 591, 603 (1944)).  A regulated utility is entitled to an 
opportunity to recover prudent operating expenses as well as capital costs, including a 
fair and reasonable rate of return on capital investments.  See Hope, 320 U.S. at 603; 
Bluefield Waterworks & Improvement Co. v. Public Service Commission of West Virginia, 
262 U.S. 679, 690 (1923) (company entitled to ask for fair return upon value of capital 
employed for public convenience); see also Duquesne Light Co. v. Barasch, 488 U.S. 
299, 310 (1989) (affirming the holding in Hope that “[i]f the total effect of the rate order 
cannot be said to be unreasonable, judicial inquiry . . . is at an end.”).  “The prudence of 
a management decision depends on good faith and reasonableness, judged at the time

the decision is made.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. Dept. of Public Utility Control, 
216 Conn. at 645. 
Ultimately, however, rate setting requires “a balancing of the investor and 
consumer interests.”  Woodbury Water Co. v. Public Utilities Commission, 174 Conn. 258, 
264 (1978) (quoting Federal Power Commission v. Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U.S. at 
603).  Further, the constitution does not bind the Authority “to the use of any single formula 
or combination of formulae in determining rates,” and the ratemaking process may involve 
“pragmatic adjustments.”  Woodbury Water Co. v. Public Utilities Commission, 174 Conn. 
at 264 (1978) (quoting Federal Power Commission v. Natural Gas Pipeline Co., 315 U.S. 
575, 586 (1942)).  In striking this balance and making pragmatic adjustments, the 
Authority is guided by the principles of General Statutes § 16-19e(a), noted above. 
III. 
MULTI-YEAR, PERFORMANCE-BASED RATE PLAN 
The Company proposes a MYPB rate plan with a four-year initial term from 
November 1, 2025, through October 31, 2029.  Application, p. 2.  The Company’s MYPB 
rate plan includes, among other things: (1) an I-X revenue adjustment mechanism; (2) a 
capital cost recovery mechanism or K-bar mechanism; (3) a “stretch factor” or consumer 
dividend; (4) an earnings sharing mechanism (ESM); (5) an exogenous events provision 
or Z-factor; and (6) performance incentive mechanisms.  Id.; Application, Ex. YGS-PBR-
1, pp. 89–90, 121–122.   
Notably, the Authority has been developing a comprehensive framework for 
performance-based regulation (PBR) with respect to electric distribution companies for 
several years and is scheduled to finalize that framework in the near future.  See Docket 
No. 21-05-15, PURA Investigation into a Performance-Based Regulation Framework for 
the Electric Distribution Companies; Docket No. 21-05-15RE01, PURA Investigation into 
Revenue Adjustment Mechanisms for a Performance-Based Regulation Framework, 
Docket No. 21-05-15RE02, PURA Investigation into Performance Mechanisms for a 
Performance-Based Regulation Framework, and Docket No. 21-05-15RE03, PURA 
Investigation into the Establishment of an Integrated Distribution System Plan within a 
Performance-Based Regulation Framework (together, PBR Framework Dockets).  Upon 
finalizing the PBR framework in those proceedings, the Authority intends to develop a 
corresponding PBR framework for the gas companies.  See General Statutes § 16-
244aa(b) (PURA “may also initiate a proceeding to investigate, develop and adopt a 
framework for implementation of performance-based regulation for gas and water 
companies”).  
PBR is an extraordinary departure from the cost-of-service (COS) ratemaking 
model employed for over a century.  Whereas COS ratemaking focuses on the prudence 
and reasonableness of a utility’s expenditures and a reasonable rate of return, PBR 
ratemaking considers outcomes, incentives, and penalties.  Other than Hawaii, no state 
has comprehensively implemented PBR.  Some states have incorporated elements of 
PBR, and others, including Connecticut, have legislation or on-going proceedings to 
establish a PBR framework.  Ultimately, PBR will likely be a hybrid model that uses 
methodologies from both the COS and PBR models.

V. 
RATE BASE 
A. 
SUMMARY 
Rate base is a fundamental principle of COS ratemaking.  Rate base is the 
investor-supplied facilities and other investments necessary to supply a utility service to 
consumers in a safe, reliable, and cost-effective manner.  For purposes of ratemaking, 
rate base is the capital on which the investor may earn a return.  See Bluefield Waterworks 
& Improvement Co. v. Public Service Commission of West Virginia, 262 U.S. at 690 (a 
“company is entitled to ask [for] a fair return upon the value of that which it employs for 
the public convenience.”). 
Cost-of-service ratemaking provides a return on rate base, which is the capital that 
has been prudently invested by shareholders and put to public use.  Id.  Consequently, 
determining rate base requires a two-prong assessment.  First, the utility must prove that 
the company’s plant is in use and is serving the public.  See Cedar Island Improvement 
Association. v. Clinton Electric Light & Power Co., 142 Conn. 359, 370 (1955) (“public 
utility company is entitled to a fair return upon the fair value of such of its property as is 
useful and being used in providing service”).  Second, the company must prove that the 
capital investment was prudent and reasonable.  See General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(5) 
(“the level and structure of rates charged customers shall reflect prudent and efficient 
management”). 
The “used and useful” standard is a “bedrock principle of utility regulation.”  
Kentucky Utilities Co. v. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 760 F.2d 1321, 1324 
n.4 (D.C. Cir. 1985).  “Generally speaking, property not employed in the public service 
should not be incorporated into the base to be used to compute the fair rate of return.  It 
must be kept in mind, however, that whether utility property is used or useful for inclusion 
in the rate base is a factual determination rather than a legal question.”  Southern New 
England Telephone Co. v. Public Utilities Commission, 29 Conn. Supp. 253, 259–60 
(1970).  The Authority does not allow for the inclusion of incomplete system additions or 
improvements into a company’s pro forma rate base.  See, e.g., Decision, May 19, 2021, 
Docket No. 20-10-31, Application of Jewett City Water Company to Amend its Rate 
Schedules, p. 23.  “[R]atepayers benefit from the plant additions when they are in-service 
and . . . ratepayers should not be responsible for providing a return on plant that is not in-
service.”).  Id., p. 24. 
Once a company has proven that property is used and useful, it must also establish 
that the capital investment was prudent and reasonable.  See General Statutes § 16-
19e(a)(5).  Specifically, “there exists a distinction between, on one hand, utility property

Docket No. 24-12-01 
 
Page 13 
 
 
and, on the other hand, the cost of utility property allowed in rate base, because only that 
portion of utility property that is the result of prudent and reasonable management is 
included in rate base.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. Dept. of Public Utility Control, 
219 Conn. 61, 68 (1991).  To demonstrate prudency, the utility must provide evidence that 
the decision to undertake the investment was reasonable at the time it was made and 
that the capital project was managed in a reasonable and cost-effective manner.  In sum, 
to establish its rate base for ratemaking purposes, the Company must demonstrate, by a 
preponderance of the evidence, that the capital proposed for inclusion in rate base (1) is 
used and useful and (2) was invested prudently. 
Rate base is calculated by taking the test year net book value of prudent capital 
investments and accounting for other factors, including accumulated depreciation, 
working capital, and non-rate base capital such as deferred taxes.  The test year is 
intended to “be representative of conditions which will probably prevail in the immediate 
future when the rates will be effective.”  Connecticut Natural Gas Corp. v. Public Utilities 
Commission, 29 Conn. Supp. at 390.  Certain pro forma adjustments may be permitted 
to recognize capital investments and other changes to rate base that occur subsequent 
to the test year.  Id., p. 390 (“company should be permitted to adjust the test year forward 
for a reasonable period of time where definitely ascertainable expenses are involved 
during such future period”).

1. Background 
Accumulated depreciation (or depreciation reserve) reflects the amount of 
depreciation expense that has been allowed in rates and accumulated to date, less any 
retirements and net salvage received as an offset to rate base.  See 22-08-08 Decision, 
p. 20; Decision, July 28, 2021, Docket No. 20-12-30, Application of the Connecticut Water 
Company to Amend its Rate Schedule (20-12-30 Decision), p. 70.  As such, the 
depreciation reserve reflects the asset deterioration of in-service plant and is maintained 
in anticipation of future asset replacement or retirement needs.  20-12-30 Decision, p. 70.  
The accumulated depreciation should be based on the depreciation rates and useful 
service lives that fall within the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners 
(NARUC) guidelines and have been allowed or approved by the Authority.  Id.  Ideally, 
assets are depreciated consistently, i.e., proportionally, with the rate of the actual 
deterioration of assets until they are retired or replaced, and the amount accumulated is 
therefore consistent with the deterioration of the asset to date and the time frame until 
retirement or replacement.  Id. 
The product of the depreciation rate and plant-in-service balance is the annual 
depreciation expense, which is recorded to reflect the annual recovery or amortization of 
previously expended capital investment.  The depreciation expense impacts the 
calculation of accumulated depreciation as any depreciation expense allowed for in rates, 
past or current, should be accounted for in some way in the calculation of accumulated 
depreciation.

As demonstrated by the preceding tables, COR has increased significantly in both

The Company asserts that the increase in COR is primarily attributable to “a 
significant increase in the amount of total capital expenditures incurred” and “the type of 
capital work performed.”  Id.  While the Authority finds it reasonable that increased total 
capital expenditures would, all things equal, increase COR expenses, the Authority is not 
persuaded that project composition explains such a substantial increase in COR. 
To support its claim that project composition drove the increase in COR, the 
Company introduced what it calls a “Historical COR Average,” calculated from “a 7-year 
historical look of capital expenditures” charged to Accounts 107 and 108 and sorted by 
project category.  Interrog. Resp. RRU-382, p. 1.  To estimate the COR expected per 
dollar of capital expenditures, the Company expressed COR as a percentage of total 
capital expenditure for each category by dividing the totals in Account 108 by those in 
Account 107 and multiplying by 100.  See Interrog. Resp. RRU-290, Att. 1.  The Company 
maintains that the Historical COR Average for each category can be used to estimate 
future COR expenses for that category, and accordingly, that the increased COR seen 
since 2021 can be attributed in part to “spend [that] has moved towards work with 
traditionally higher COR.”  Interrog. Resp. 290, p. 1. 
The Authority finds this manner of estimate unreliable under the circumstances 
because the “7-year historical look” includes the post-2020 years of elevated COR.  See 
id.  By incorporating the elevated years into the benchmark used to estimate future costs, 
the increase is effectively embedded into the benchmark used to justify the increase.  A 
benchmark so distorted by the increase under review cannot serve as a neutral proxy for 
average COR. 
In addition, the composition component of the Company’s analysis lacks sufficient 
evidentiary support.  Specifically, the Company treats any increase in COR not explained 
by higher total capital expenditures as a residual and attributes the entire residual to 
“increased work on higher COR projects.”  Interrog. Resp. RRU-382, Att. 2.  The 
assumption that the entire remaining COR increase is attributable to the change in project 
composition is unjustified and unsupported by the record due to possible alternative 
influences, such as (but not limited to) project execution error or accounting 
misclassifications.  Without quantifying and excluding other possible confounding factors, 
the use of the residual amounts to a mathematical convenience, not a causal finding. 
For these reasons, the Authority rejects the Company’s project composition 
analysis.  The record does not support the assertion that project composition explains the 
magnitude of the post-2020 COR increase.  Accordingly, the Authority considered 
normalizing the COR for 2021 through 2024 by applying the 2018–2020 average COR-

2. Cash Working Capital 
a. Summary 
It is customary regulatory practice to allow an adjustment to rate base in 
recognition of the timing difference between when revenues are received and when 
expenses are paid out.  This timing difference is known as CWC.  CWC represents “the 
amount of cash needed by Yankee to fund its day-to-day operations in the time period 
between when expenses are incurred to provide service to customers, and when

Docket No. 24-12-01 
 
Page 31 
 
 
associated cash payment is actually received from customers for those services.”  
Application, Ex. YGS-REVREQ-1 (Revenue Requirements Panel PFT), p. 118. 
The Company proposed $28,169,000 as its allowance for CWC.  Late Filed Ex. 1-
SP03, Ex. 2, Sch. B-1.0.  The Authority approves a CWC allowance of $16,428,750. 
b. Lead / Lag Study 
For larger utilities, the Authority established a preference that a lead/lag study be 
conducted to determine the appropriate CWC allowance, rather than rely on a heuristic 
approach such as a percentage of expenses.  A lead/lag study is a common method for 
developing the CWC component of rate base in a rate case.  Here, the Company included 
a lead/lag study in the Application.  See generally Revenue Requirements Panel PFT, Ex. 
YGS-REVREQ-2-H Schedules, Sch. H-1.4.  The lead lag study quantifies (1) the revenue 
lag days, which represent the number of days between when Yankee customers receive 
service and when Yankee receives payment for that service; and (2) the expense lead 
days, which represent the number of days between when Yankee receives goods or 
services from vendors and when it pays for those goods or services.  Revenue 
Requirements Panel PFT, p. 119.  The difference between the revenue lag days and the 
expense lead days results in a net lag/lead day amount that is then multiplied by the 
average daily expense for each cost category.  Id.  The sum of these products is the 
Company’s proposed CWC component of rate base.  Id. 
c. Purchased Gas Cost Related Revenue Lag 
The Company’s proposed CWC improperly includes revenue lag days from 
Purchased Gas Adjustment (PGA) revenues.  The Company takes the position that the 
PGA model does not produce the daily cash inflows and outflows relevant to a lead/lag 
study and instead “reconciles actual billed revenues to actual purchased gas costs.”  
Revenue Requirements Panel PFT, pp. 133, 138.  The Company notes that the PGA 
model’s use of billed instead of accrued sales “does not cause the Company to receive 
cash from the customer any faster, because the Company only receives the cash from 
customers when customers pay their bills.”  Id., p. 135. 
However, the Authority previously found that billing and service lags associated 
with PGA revenues are eliminated due to the true-up and recovery mechanism of the PGA 
clause.  Specifically, the Authority found that “the PGA effectively aligns meter reads and 
subsequent billings with service rendered, and eliminates the service and billing lags.”  
Decision, Jan. 22, 2014, Docket No. 13-06-08, Application of Connecticut Natural Gas 
Corporation to Increase Its Rates and Charges (13-06-08 Decision), p. 7.  This approach 
was also adopted in the 23-11-02 CNG Decision.  23-11-02 CNG Decision, pp. 26–27. 
In the most recent Yankee rate case that directly addressed this issue, the 
Authority found that: 
The issue is not the difference in the amount of recovery; it is the difference 
in the timing of recovery.  The Company’s PGA recovers accrued purchased 
gas costs based on billed revenues . . . In moving from accrued sales to

Docket No. 24-12-01

billed sales, Yankee has not changed its billing cycles, when it reads its 
meters, when it sends out its bills or anything else related to its billing 
process.  What has changed is the accounting timing of its recovery of 
purchased gas costs.  This timing difference was/is effectuated by the one-
time adjustment and the continuing over- and under-recoveries that are 
reconciled through the PGA.  No longer are accrued revenues recovering 
accrued purchased gas costs; now billed revenues are recovering these 
accrued costs . . . .  
Decision, June 29, 2011, Docket No. 10-12-02, Application of Yankee Gas Services 
Company for Amended Rate Schedules, pp. 36–37 (10-12-02 Decision).32

Therefore, the Company’s position is that the actual cash received from the

incurred in August 2023.  This is a net cash lag.

rather a cash lead of at eight days.  In the foregoing example, the Company receives

PROXY GROUP 
The Authority identified a group of 10 prospective companies to ascertain the 
market-based range of the cost of equity for the Company.  The Authority uses certain 
criteria (Authority Screening Criteria) to identify companies that have risk and investment 
profiles similar to the Company’s.  Generally, a company will be considered a proxy 
company if it: (1) derives at least 70% of revenue from regulated utilities, as reported by 
Value Line; (2) derives at least 50% of regulated revenue from regulated gas distribution, 
as reported by Value Line; (3) is publicly traded and reported by Value Line; (4) has paid 
consistent dividends for eight quarters and is expected to continue; (5) is not in financial 
distress; (6) is not the target of an acquisition or merger activity; (7) has credit ratings that 
are at least investment grade, as determined by S&P Global (BBB- and above) and/or 
Moody’s Investor Service (Moody’s) (Baa3 and above); and (8) is not projected to have 
negative earnings growth as reported by Value Line.  See 23-11-02 CNG Decision, pp. 
42–43. 
Applying the Authority Screening Criteria produces a proxy group that has similar 
revenues and a similar credit profile to the company being analyzed as well as robust 
data to use in the cost of equity methodologies.  The Authority considered the proxy 
groups proposed by the Company, OCC, and EOE.  All parties recommended proxy group 
companies consisting of publicly traded gas and electric companies followed by Value 
Line. 
To develop its proposed proxy group, the Company began with a group of 10 
investor-owned domestic natural gas distribution companies covered by Value Line.  
Application, Ex. YGS-ROE-1 (Cost of Capital Panel PFT), p. 28.  The Company then

(1) Consistently pays quarterly cash dividends because it is a necessary

S&P to ensure the proxy companies have a comparable financial risk profile 
to that of the Company; 
(3) Is covered by more than one equity analyst to ensure that estimates are 
consensus based; 
(4) Has positive earnings growth rates, which is a necessary assumption in the 
DCF model, published by at least two of the following sources: Value Line,

3. Capital Structure Analysis 
The Authority establishes the ratemaking capital structure by carefully weighing 
several factors, including: the actual capital structure of the utility and its parent company, 
the range of capital structures of the proxy group, and the credit rating agency metrics.  
The Authority is obligated to balance both investor and consumer interests in reaching a 
determination on the appropriate capital structure.  Woodbury Water Co., 174 Conn. at 
264.  Generally, the utility will advocate for a higher equity component in its capital 
structure because a higher equity component generally provides a higher return for its 
investors.  At the same time, a higher equity component also decreases the financial risk 
of the Company as it holds less debt in its capital structure.  Conversely, parties such as

Docket No. 24-12-01 
 
Page 47 
 
 
OCC will often advocate for a lower equity component in the Company's capitalization 
structure because debt is generally less expensive for ratepayers than equity. 
However, investor and consumer interests in capital structure are not entirely 
divergent.  Specifically, a capital structure with too little equity could maximize the benefits 
of lower cost debt but would ultimately increase the Company’s risk profile and, hence, 
the cost of equity.  On the other hand, a capital structure with too much equity would 
unnecessarily burden ratepayers with a more expensive capital structure and not achieve 
the lowest cost of capital for the Company that balances both risk and the overall cost of 
capital.  Consequently, the Authority must account for a variety of factors to find an optimal 
capitalization mix for the Company’s cost of capital.

1. Summary 
The Authority finds that a net ROE of 9.32% reflects a commensurate rate of return

environment, and the level of service and management provided by the Company.  
Specifically, the Authority finds that an unadjusted ROE of 9.48% provides a utility that

2. Discounted Cash Flow Model 
a. Discounted Cash Flow Model Description 
The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model is a market-based financial model that 
attempts to replicate the valuation process used by investors.  The DCF model assumes 
that investors evaluate stocks in a classical economic framework and buy and sell 
securities rationally at prices that reflect the assets’ value.  Under the DCF model, the 
value of a financial asset is based upon the present value principle.  Specifically, the

Docket No. 24-12-01 
 
Page 52 
 
 
present value of a financial asset equals the discounted value of its expected future cash 
flows.  Investors discount these expected cash flows at their required rate of return (i.e., 
the cost of equity or ROE).  Therefore, by using proxy company data, the DCF model 
provides evidence of commensurate ROEs for utilities with corresponding risk profiles. 
The traditional constant growth DCF model requires the following assumptions: a 
constant growth rate for earnings and dividends; a stable dividend payout ratio; a constant 
price-to-earnings ratio; and a discount rate greater than the expected growth rate. 
The DCF model is represented by the formula of K = D1 / Po + G, where: 
K = the market-required ROE; 
D1 = the forecasted dividend paid one period into the future; 
Po = an estimate to the current market price of the stock; and 
G = investors’ long-run growth expectations. 
In short, the ROE (K) can be determined by summing the expected dividend yield 
(D1/Po) and the expected growth rate (G). 
b. Expected Growth Rate 
The Authority first considers the expected growth rate for the companies in the 
Authority Proxy Group because the expected growth rate is also a factor in calculating 
the expected dividend yield.  The constant growth form of the DCF model assumes a 
single growth estimate in perpetuity.  To reduce the expected growth rate to a single 
measure, the constant payout ratio, EPS, dividends per share (DPS), and book value per 
share (BVPS) are assumed to all grow at the same constant rate.  The distinction between 
the parties’ approaches to the expected growth rate is (1) the specific growth measures 
considered and (2) the weighting of the measures.

c. Expected Dividend Yield 
The second input into the DCF model is the Expected Dividend Yield.  For 
purposes of the DCF model, the Expected Dividend Yield is estimated by taking a

duration of time and does not reflect any significant market disruptions that might

3. Capital Asset Pricing Model 
a. Capital Asset Pricing Model Description 
The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) evaluates the relationship between the 
expected return and risk of investing in a security and can be used to calculate the 
expected return of an asset.  Therefore, like the DCF model, by incorporating proxy 
company data, the CAPM provides evidence of commensurate ROEs for utilities with 
corresponding risk profiles.  To determine the cost of equity, the CAPM first determines 
the appropriate risk-free rate and then adds a beta, or the degree of co-movement of the 
security’s rate of return with the market’s rate of return, multiplied by the expected equity 
risk premium (ERP), which is the amount by which investors expect the future return on 
equities, in general, to exceed that on the risk-free asset.

The CAPM model is represented by the formula Ke = Rf + β (Rm-Rf), where: 
Ke = the required market ROE; 
β = Beta coefficient of an individual security; 
Rf = the risk-free rate of return; and 
Rm = the required return on the market; the term (Rm - Rf) represents the ERP. 
Consequently, once the Beta (β) and ERP (Rm- Rf) are determined, an ROE can 
be calculated.

measure because it requires an estimate of the expected Rm).

4. Expected Earnings Analysis 
The Company proposed using an expected earnings model for determining ROE.  
Cost of Capital Panel PFT, pp. 45–47.  The Expected Earnings methodology is a 
comparable earnings analysis that calculates the earnings that an investor expects to 
receive on the book value of a stock.  Id.  The use of an Expected Earnings approach 
based on the proxy companies provides a range of the expected returns on a group of 
risk-comparable companies to the subject company.  Id.   
The Authority has previously declined this Cost of Equity methodology.  See, e.g., 
22-07-01 Decision, pp. 52–53.  The rationale for rejecting the methodology is consistent 
with arguments made by the EOE witness.  EOE claims that the approach is flawed as it 
does not measure the cost of equity demanded by investors in the market instead, it relies 
on projected accounting return on book equity.  Rothschild PFT, p. 95.  The returns on 
book equity are not the returns of the investor, however.  Id.  As such, investors earn 
returns on the market price of a stock, not the book value of a stock.  Id. 
The Authority finds that the Expected Earnings approach does not measure market 
cost of equity as it is accounting-based and not a measure of investors’ market-based 
required returns.  Consequently, the Authority rejects the Expected Earnings approach. 
5. Bond Yield Risk Premium 
The Company also proposed using the bond yield plus risk premium (BYPRP) 
model for determining ROE.  Cost of Capital Panel PFT, pp. 41–45.  The Company 
described the BYPRP as an estimation of the cost of equity as the sum of the equity risk 
premium and the yield on a particular class of bonds to illustrate the fundamental principle 
that equity investors bear the residual risk associated with equity ownership and thus, 
require a premium over a bond return.  Id., pp. 41–42.  The risk premium analysis reflects 
an inverse relationship between interest rates and the equity risk premium and should 
rely on recent and expected market conditions.  Id.  For its analysis the Company used

Docket No. 24-12-01 
 
Page 67 
 
 
actual authorized returns for gas utilities as the historical measure of the cost of equity to 
determine the risk premium.  Cost of Capital Panel PFT, p. 42.  The analysis developed 
a “regression equation of the risk premium as a function of U.S. Treasury bond yields, 
with authorized gas utility ROEs serve as a measure of required equity returns.”  Id.  The 
Company defines the risk premium as “the difference between authorized gas utility 
ROEs and U.S. Treasury bond yields.”  Id.   
OCC points out several problems with the Company’s BYPRP analysis.  First, it is 
a measure of Commission behavior and not investor behavior.  Woolridge PFT, p. 94.  
Second, the Company’s analysis “produces inflated measures of the risk premium 
because it uses historic authorized ROEs and Treasury yields, and the resulting risk 
premium is applied to projected Treasury Yields.”  Id.  Third, since utility stocks are selling 
above book value for the last decade, OCC claims authorized ROEs are above what 
investors require as measured by this metric.  Id., p. 95.  Finally, under the Company’s 
analysis the resulting ROE is dependent on authorized ROE’s from state utility 
commissions and OCC claims that over the past forty years, authorized ROE’s have not 
decreased in proportion to capital costs and have exaggerated the actual cost of equity 
capital.  Id. 
The Authority reaffirms its determination that the BYPRP approach is not widely 
accepted today in utility ratemaking as this benchmarking-comparison methodology has 
been replaced by regulators with market-based approaches, such as DCF or CAPM.  
The Authority most recently rejected the BYPRP approach in the 22-07-01 
Decision.  At that time, the Authority reconsidered the risk premium plus approaches that 
used Commission-allowed ROEs as inputs and found the methodology was highly 
dependent on the number of companies included in the proxy group and the time-period 
covered.  22-07-01 Decision, pp. 52–53.  The Authority further found that the approach 
was not a measure of investors’ market-based required returns but an assessment of 
prior regulatory commission behavior.  Id.  Consequently, since no evidence or rationale 
has been offered to the contrary, the Authority again rejects any approach using 
commission-allowed ROEs as the input data, including the BYPRP model.  
6. Comparable Allowed ROEs 
Although the Authority will not consider financial models based on other public 
utility commission allowed ROEs, the Authority will examine the ROEs approved in other 
jurisdictions.  However, the authorized ROE should reflect the economic and financial 
conditions expected during the Rate Year.  Previously allowed ROEs are, by their nature, 
not based on the most current financial data and generally provide a historical snapshot 
only.  Because allowed ROEs from other jurisdictions are historical and do not necessarily 
reflect current market conditions, the Authority finds that such allowed ROEs are limited 
to serving only as a point of reference. 
To that end, the Authority reviewed data on authorized ROEs nationwide by 
Regulatory Research Associates (RRA).  RRA provides ROE data disaggregated by, 
among other things, case type (e.g., all cases, general rate cases, limited issue riders),

or fully litigated cases).  
According to S&P Capital IQ, in 2024, the average authorized ROE was 9.72%.  
Interrog. Resp. RRU-395-SP01.  This is up slightly from 2023 as the average authorized 
ROE in 2023 was 9.64%.  Id.  Additionally, as of June 25, 2025, the date of the submitted 
interrogatory, the average was 9.73%.  Id.  For purposes of the instant proceeding, the 
Authority focused on the distribution-only cross section because the Company is a gas 
distribution utility.  Vertically integrated utilities are not comparable to the Company and 
are riskier due to their generation functions. 
Additionally, the Authority reviewed data on authorized ROEs presented by OCC.  
The average annual authorized ROEs for gas distribution companies were 9.47% in 2020, 
9.56% in 2021, 9.53% in 2022, 9.64% in 2023, and 9.72% in 2024.  Woolridge PFT, p. 
73. 
OCC referenced a 2022 Werner and Jarvis study evaluating the authorized ROEs 
in 3,500 electric and gas rate case decisions in the U.S. from 1980 to 2021.  Woolridge 
PFT, p. 22; Karl Dunkle Werner and Stephen Jarvis, “Rate of Return Regulation 
Revisited,” Working Paper, Energy Institute, University of California at Berkeley, 2022.  
This study compared the allowed ROE to capital cost benchmarks including government 
and corporate bonds, CAPM equity cost rate estimates, and United Kingdom (UK) 
authorized ROEs.  Id.  The study focused on the following three questions: (1) to what 
extent are utilities being allowed to earn excess return by their regulators, (2) how has 
this return effects utilities capital investment decisions and (3) what impact has this had 
on cost to ratepayers.  Id.  As previously discussed in Section VI.E.5. Bond Risk Premium, 
OCC asserts that, over the last four decades, authorized ROEs have not decreased in 
proportion to capital costs.  Woolridge PFT, p. 23.  As a result, previous authorized ROEs 
have overestimated the true cost of equity.  Id.  Consequently, OCC argues that a 
recommended ROE below those from other jurisdictions is reasonable.  Id.  
Overall, because allowed ROEs from other jurisdictions are historical and do not 
necessarily reflect current market conditions, the Authority finds that such allowed ROEs 
are limited to serving only as a point of reference.

operating company level.  See Section XII, Environmental, Social, and Governance 
Practices, infra.  As documented in this proceeding, Yankee’s workplace diversity and 
inclusion efforts lack company-specific structure and accountability.  Programs are 
delivered at the enterprise level and are not anchored to Yankee-specific goals or 
benchmarks, limiting transparency into whether these initiatives improve representation 
or advancement opportunities within Yankee’s workforce.  Similarly, the Company’s 
voluntary training programs and broad recruitment networks are not linked to operating 
company metrics or outcomes, preventing stakeholders from assessing whether 
ratepayer-funded expenditures deliver equitable workforce results.

regulatory requirements, is focused on legacy manufactured gas plant sites and does not 
demonstrate integration with broader ESG commitments such as proactive community 
environmental benefits or equitable stakeholder engagement.  Taken together, these gaps 
show that high enterprise-level ESG scores do not necessarily translate into meaningful, 
measurable ESG outcomes at Yankee itself.

financially from its ESG standing, these advantages are already captured in existing credit 
ratings and investor interest.  Therefore, there is no basis to increase Yankee’s ROE on 
the grounds of ESG performance absent demonstrated, operating company-specific 
implementation that produces tangible environmental and equity outcomes for the 
customers who fund its operations.

10. Reductions to ROE 
a. Summary 
Having found that a 9.48% ROE is reasonable for a similarly situated gas utility 
providing expert, efficient, and prudent management of the utility franchise, the Authority 
considered whether to adjust the ROE for the Company’s actual management of its 
franchise and concludes that a cumulative 16 basis point reduction to the Company’s 
ROE is necessary to reflect the Company’s deficient performance in managing certain 
parts of its utility franchise and to incentivize the Company to improve its performance.  
The interrelationship between investor returns and utility performance is well-established.  
Importantly, the “rate-making process . . . involves a balancing of the investor and the 
consumer interests.”  Hope, 320 U.S. at 603.  Similarly, a utility’s rate of return should be 
“reasonably sufficient to assure confidence in the financial soundness of the utility and 
should be adequate, under efficient and economical management, to maintain and 
support its credit and enable it to raise the money necessary for the proper discharge of 
its public duties.”  Bluefield, 262 U.S. at 692–93 (emphasis added). 
Indeed, courts interpreting the “under efficient and economical management” 
language in Bluefield have determined that a utility’s rate of return may be adjusted to 
account for imprudent and inefficient management.  In re Citizens Utilities Co., 171 Vt. 
447, 460-61 (2000) (“Like Vermont, most other jurisdictions now accept the general 
principle that rates may be adjusted depending on the adequacy of the utility's service 
and the efficiency of its management.”); D.C. Transit System, Inc. v. Washington 
Metropolitan Area Transit Comm., 466 F.2d 394, 423 (D.C. Cir. 1972) (“We believe the

Docket No. 24-12-01 
 
Page 79 
 
 
constitutionality of governmental recognition of the interrelationship between fair return 
and quality service can hardly be doubted today.”); see also Richard J. Pierce & Emest 
Gellhorn, Regulated Industries in a Nutshell, pp. 134–35 (3d ed. 1994) (“The phrase 
‘under efficient and economical management’ [in Bluefield] is an important qualification.  
If an agency finds that a firm is not being managed efficiently and economically, it can 
lower the firm’s allowed rate of return below the level otherwise required to meet the 
comparable risk test.”). 
In Connecticut, the statutes governing rates reflect this important balance.  On one 
hand, “the level and structure of rates [must] be sufficient, but no more than sufficient, to 
allow public service companies to cover their operating costs including, but not limited to, 
appropriate staffing levels, and capital costs, to attract needed capital and to maintain 
their financial integrity, . . .”  General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4).  On the other, the Company 
has an affirmative obligation to be “technically, financially and managerially expert and 
efficient,” and must perform its “public responsibilities with economy [and] efficiency” and 
rates must “reflect prudent and efficient management of the franchise.”  General Statutes 
§ 16-19e(a)(2), (3), and (5).  This constitutional and statutory balance is the foundation of 
the so-called “regulatory compact” between regulators and investor-owned utilities.  In a 
quid pro quo, the utilities are entitled to recover operating expenses and reasonable return 
on capital, and ratepayers, in exchange, are entitled to expert, efficient, and prudent 
management. 
Consequently, if a utility fails to uphold its end of the bargain by not providing 
expert, efficient, and prudent management, the regulator must adjust the scales to 
maintain the balance required by Hope, Bluefield, and General Statutes § 16-19e(a).  One 
way to accomplish this rebalancing is to reduce a utility’s allowed ROE.  See, e.g., 
Decision, December 17, 2014, Docket No. 14-05-06, Application by The Connecticut Light 
and Power Company to Amend Rate Schedules, p. 152 (ordering a 15 basis point ROE 
reduction for deficient storm response); Decision, April 27, 2011, Docket No. 10-09-08, 
Application of United Water Connecticut, Inc. to Amend Rate Schedules, p. 83 (ordering 
a 50 basis point ROE reduction for imprudent management of accounting, record keeping, 
and billing methods). 
An ROE adjustment is not a penalty for a specific act; rather, it serves as a 
mechanism to set rates commensurate with the level of service the ratepayers are 
receiving and, more generally, with the company’s adherence to its broader public 
responsibilities.  See In re Citizens Utilities Co., 171 Vt. at 454 (“the purpose of a rate-of-
return reduction is not to penalize a company for specific acts of misconduct, but rather 
to set reasonable rates in cases where the consumers are not being adequately served 
due to inefficiency or improvidence or other like reasons.”). 
In this proceeding, the Authority identified several areas in which the Company’s 
performance did not reflect expert, efficient, and prudent management.  The Authority and 
parties engaged in a robust discovery process, culminating in eight days of hearings, the 
filing of late filed exhibits and subsequent late filed exhibit hearings, and post-hearing 
briefs and reply briefs.  Evidence from this lengthy adjudicatory process led the Authority

11. Approved ROE 
In determining a reasonable ROE, the Authority considers the analytical models 
for commensurate utility returns, allowed ROEs in other jurisdictions, the prevailing 
market conditions, and the Company’s risk profile.  The Authority considers the two 
analytical models (DCF and CAPM) to provide a target range for commensurate ROEs.  
The Authority generally weighs the DCF model results more heavily than the CAPM 
results because the DCF model relies on directly observable proxy company market data 
and provides a better measure of the cost of equity for similarly situated utilities.  
Conversely, the CAPM relies primarily on risk-premium studies and market predictions, 
which are more subjective in nature. 
Here, the DCF model as applied to the Authority Proxy Group indicates an ROE 
range of 8.56% to 10.89%, with an average of 9.48%.  The CAPM model produced an 
ROE range of 8.95% to 9.37%, with an average of 9.17%

Given this range, the Authority must determine an ROE such that the Company 
has an opportunity to “cover . . . [its] capital costs, to attract needed capital and to maintain 
[its] financial integrity.”  General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(4).  This statutory standard reflects 
the long-standing principle that “the return to the equity owner should be commensurate 
with returns on investments in other enterprises having corresponding risks and should 
also be sufficient to assure confidence in the financial integrity of the enterprise, so as to 
maintain its credit and to attract capital.”  Connecticut Light & Power Co. v. Dept. of Public 
Utility Control, 216 Conn. at 634–35.  In determining an ROE, the Authority “is not bound 
to the use of any single formula or combination of formulae” but again must balance 
“investor and consumer interests” and make “pragmatic adjustments.”  Woodbury Water 
Co., 174 Conn. at 264. 
Cognizant of this legal framework, the Authority has analyzed a wide array of 
considerations in reaching a determination, including, without limitation, the Company’s 
capital structure, its financial condition, ROEs from other jurisdictions, analytical models 
of commensurate returns, prevailing and anticipated market conditions, risk factors, and 
the regulatory environment.  The Company is financially stable, with a credit rating of BBB 
from S&P, and a Baa1 rating from Moody’s.  In addition, the Company operates in a 
regulatory environment that reduces risk through the Distribution Integrity Management 
Program (DIMP) mechanism and the revenue decoupling adjustment.  Considering these 
and other factors, the Authority adopts a 9.48% ROE.  Accounting for the 16 basis point 
reduction, the Authority approves a 9.32% ROE.

Allowable O&M expenses must “reflect prudent and efficient management of the 
franchise operation.”  General Statutes § 16-19e(a)(5).  Therefore, those expenses that 
are reasonable and necessary to provide service to the public may be included as an 
allowable expense.  The Company has the burden of proving that expenses under 
consideration for inclusion in rates are just and reasonable.  See General Statutes § 16-
22.  In addition to being prudent, pro forma adjustments must be “known and measurable” 
and supported by a preponderance of evidence, with the burden resting on the utility to 
make such a showing.  See Connecticut Natural Gas Corp. v. Dept. of Public Utility 
Control, 51 Conn. Supp. 307, 322 (2009) (affirming agency’s decision that, in part, applied 
the “known and measurable” standard to pro forma adjustments); see also Aquarion 
Water Company of Connecticut v. Public Utilities Regulatory Authority, No. HHB-CV-23-
6078177-S, 2024 WL 1403433, at *9 (Conn. Super. Ct. Mar. 25, 2024) (application of 
known and measurable standard for depreciation is within PURA’s regulatory discretion).  
Consequently, the Authority will consider reasonable historical test year expenses, as 
adjusted for known and measurable changes, to determine a utility’s allowable expenses.

Employees of Yankee and employees, officers, and executives of EESCO receive 
cash incentive compensation under EESCO’s Employee Annual Incentive Program.  See 
Interrog. Resp. OCC-127, Att. 6.  In order for employees of Yankee and employees, 
officers, and executives of EESCO to receive cash incentive compensation, EESCO must 
first establish the variable compensation pool, which is used to fund both employee and 
officer cash incentive compensation.  Hr’g Tr., 526:15–19.  The amount by which EESCO 
funds the variable compensation pool each year is based on EESCO’s achievement of 
the targets on the Eversource Target Performance Scorecard, which the EESCO 
Executive Compensation Committee sets annually.  Interrog. Resp. OCC-135; 
Application, Ex. YGS-EMPLOYEE-1 (Employee Benefits and Compensation Panel PFT), 
pp. 27–28.  Notably, 70% of the targets on the Eversource Target Performance Scorecard 
are based on the achievement of financial goals and 30% are based on the achievement 
of operational goals.  Hr’g Tr., 525:23–526:18.  If EESCO achieves some or all of the 
targets, it funds the variable compensation pool.  Interrog. Resp. OCC-457.  Conversely, 
if EESCO fails to achieve any of the targets, it would not fund the variable compensation 
pool and, as such, would not pay out employee and officer cash incentive compensation.  
Interrog. Resp. OCC-135; Employee Benefits and Compensation Panel PFT, p. 26.  
Notably, the Company states that it would be a “highly unusual occurrence” for EESCO 
to make a determination to not fund the variable funding pool.  Interrog. Resp. OCC-457, 
p. 1.  According to the Company, “it would take . . . a catastrophe to not pay or even be 
at the 80 percent level.”  Hr’g Tr., 528:23–529:1. 
Once EESCO determines the amount of the variable compensation pool, it 
distributes the funding evenly to all managers based on each manager’s employee count.  
Id., 553:1–14.  Managers then distribute the cash incentive compensation to their 
employees based on the amount of funding received by the manager and each 
employee’s performance and incentive opportunity range.  Interrog. Resp. OCC-127, Att. 
6, p. 1.  The amount of cash incentive compensation an employee may receive is 
determined based on the employee’s base pay and target incentive level, which the 
employee’s manager then adjusts based on the manager’s assessment of the employee’s 
individual performance.  Hr’g Tr., 529:24–530:10.  An employee’s target cash incentive 
level is 100%; however, an employee may receive cash incentive compensation between 
0% and 200% of the employee’s target cash incentive level depending on performance, 
the amount of cash incentive compensation received by the manager, and the 
performance of other employees in the same department.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-24, p. 6.

executives, and officers will not receive any incentive compensation even if they are high 
performers (and even though customers are paying for the cash incentive compensation 
through rates).  Lastly, the goals on the Eversource Target Performance Scorecard 
identified as operational include goals not applicable to gas companies, such as the 
months between interruptions or MBI goal, the customer average interruption duration 
index or duration of outages or CAIDI goal, and the system average interruption duration 
index or SAIDI goal.  Hr’g Tr., 523:20–524:12; Employee Benefits and Compensation 
Panel PFT, p. 28.  Indeed, only one of the goals on the Eversource Target Performance 
Scorecard is applicable only to gas companies.  Id. 
In addition, the “external checks” the Company uses to ensure the appropriateness 
of the variable compensation pool goals align with the interests of shareholders, not 
ratepayers.  Specifically, the Company testified that the EESCO Executive Compensation 
Committee “must demonstrate to shareholders that compensation is correlated to 
performance.”  Employee Benefits and Compensation Panel PFT, p. 29.  However, as 
OCC argues, “[t]he Company does not attempt to explain how Eversource shareholders 
are qualified or capable of determining whether incentive compensation plan goals are 
‘appropriate’ in the context of the recovery of associated costs from ratepayers—as 
opposed to shareholders.”  OCC Brief, pp. 138–139.  The Company also referenced 
recommendations made by Institutional Shareholder Services (ISS) to institutional 
investors as one of its “external checks,” but admitted that ISS’s focus is solely on 
shareholders, not ratepayers.92  Hr’g Tr., 682:11–23; Employee Benefits and 
Compensation Panel PFT, p. 29.  In addition, the Company testified it relies on customers 
as an “external check” as customers “would be quick to identify any perceived failure to 
provide that level of service.”  Employee Benefits and Compensation Panel PFT, p. 29.  
As stated by OCC, “[w]hile it is true that customers can ‘identify’ concerns, the Company 
lacks any incentive to respond to its customers—this, after all, is the whole point of 
economic regulation . . . .  [I]t is precisely because customers cannot act as an “external 
check” on the Company’s actions that this very rate case exists.”  OCC Brief, p. 139.  
Consequently, the Company’s “external checks” on the appropriateness of its cash 
incentive compensation goals are focused exclusively on shareholders and prioritize 
accountability to shareholders over customers. 
Additionally, the evidence in the record does not support a finding that the 
employee and officer cash incentive compensation properly incentivizes employees, 
executives, and officers in such a way that it constitutes prudent and efficient 
management of the Company’s franchise operation.  Specifically, the Company provided

b. Remediation History 
i. 
Manufactured Gas Plant (MGP) Sites 
Yankee owns 14 former manufactured gas plant (MGP) sites across its service 
territory, one of which, Winsted, is shared with CL&P.  Environmental Panel PFT, p. 9.  
These sites were acquired through mergers and acquisitions of predecessor companies.  
Id.  Contamination associated with MGP sites includes residual byproducts from historical 
gasification operations, such as tar, hydrocarbon sludge, spent oxide waste, coke, ash, 
non-aqueous phase liquids, distillate products, and light-end oils.  Environmental Panel 
PFT, p. 9, n. 8.  These contaminants may affect soils, groundwater, surface water, and 
sediments, requiring investigation and remediation to meet State and federal 
environmental standards.  Id., p. 10. 
Federal and state regulatory requirements drive remediation efforts, including the 
Federal Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act and 
State programs such as the Remediation Standard Regulations, the Connecticut Transfer 
Act, Significant Environmental Hazard regulations, Consent Orders, and the Voluntary 
Remediation Program (VRP).  Id., pp. 10–11.  These programs also require 
post-remediation actions, including groundwater monitoring, soil vapor monitoring, and 
maintenance of engineered controls.  Id., p. 11.  
The timing of cleanup activities is influenced by regulatory requirements, local 
government objectives, and site-specific conditions, including the need to monitor 
remediation effectiveness before pursuing additional work.  Environmental Panel PFT, p. 
13.  Yankee coordinates with state and municipal officials to align remediation schedules 
with community development plans, which can reduce costs and support revitalization 
opportunities.  Id., p. 15. 
To illustrate Yankee’s work, the Company provided details for several sites 
addressed through interrogatory responses, including Willimantic, Bristol, and Danbury.  
Id., p. 16; Interrog. Resp. UPA-17; Interrog. Resp. UPA-18; Interrog. Resp. UPA-19. 
ii. Willimantic MGP 
The Willimantic MGP entered the VRP in 2015.  Environmental Panel PFT, p. 15.  
Investigation and remediation were completed ahead of schedule on November 21, 2023,

Docket No. 24-12-01 
 
Page 136 
 
 
and post-remediation groundwater monitoring began in July 2024, one year earlier than 
planned.  Id.  The remediation project included vegetation clearing, removal of 
construction debris, excavation of approximately 15,000 tons of impacted soil, installation 
of a four-foot cap, retaining wall repairs adjacent to the Willimantic River, perimeter 
fencing, topsoil placement, and hydro-seeding.  Id., p. 16. 
Initial groundwater sampling identified concentrations exceeding surface water 
protection criteria in two bedrock wells, prompting evaluation of supplemental in situ 
chemical oxidation options.  Id.  Yankee explained that any chemical oxidation program 
would require a bench-scale study to determine effectiveness and dosing, and regulatory 
approval would not be sought until at least 2026 after one year of quarterly 
post-remediation monitoring.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-17, pp. 1–2. 
iii. Bristol MGP 
The Bristol MGP entered the VRP in 2008, and soil remediation was completed in 
2012.  Environmental Panel PFT, p. 16.  Groundwater compliance monitoring continues 
due to residual impacts beneath site boundaries and State Route 6, where concentrations 
remain above State criteria.  Id.  Yankee performs annual sampling to track 
improvements, with plans to increase to quarterly monitoring once compliance appears 
feasible.  Id., p. 17.   
Annual sampling has shown a downward trend in contaminant concentrations, but 
2024 testing still detected exceedances in four monitoring wells near State Route 6.  
Interrog. Resp. UPA-18.  Yankee stated it would continue annual sampling until the 
release-based cleanup regulations are finalized, expected in early 2026.  Id.  At that time, 
the Company would evaluate additional measures such as engineered caps, 
pump-and-treat systems, in-situ injection options, or installation of new wells to better 
define exceedances.  Id.  
iv. Danbury MGP 
Yankee plans to enter the Danbury MGP into the VRP; however, entry is delayed 
due to the City of Danbury’s interest in acquiring the property through eminent domain.  
Environmental Panel PFT, p. 23.  Additional investigation was already required after 
identifying three Significant Environmental Hazard conditions in shallow soils, which were 
removed and closed in 2019.  Id. 
From 2021 to 2023, supplemental Phase III work included test trenching, soil 
sampling, and installation of three bedrock monitoring wells, with reporting completed in 
2022 and a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment completed in 2023.  Id.  Remaining 
below-grade source material and historic structures must be removed before 
redevelopment, and certain site areas may require vapor mitigation systems and use 
restrictions limiting future land use to industrial or commercial purposes.  Interrog. Resp. 
UPA-19, p. 1.  These conditions could affect property value and compensation if the City 
of Danbury acquires the property through eminent domain.  Id.  If the City proceeds, it 
would assume primary remediation responsibility, although Eversource may still retain 
obligations for legacy contamination under state law.  Id., p. 2.

v. Community Coordination and Emerging Issues 
Yankee coordinates remediation with municipal plans through its Community 
Relations Department, which regularly meets with municipalities to align schedules, 
obtain permits, and minimize public disruption.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-20.  Examples 
include site capping in Shelton to create public parking and collaboration with Danbury 
on a proposed transit hub.  Id.  
Regarding emerging concerns, Yankee monitors DEEP’s draft RBCRs, having 
engaged in their development through stakeholder participation and written comments.  
Interrog. Resp. UPA-21.  The Company expects the new regulations could extend closure 
timelines and increase post-remediation groundwater monitoring costs but does not 
anticipate altering its investigation or remediation approach.  Id.   
vi. Post-Remediation Monitoring and Timeline 
After completing remediation (e.g., soil excavation, in-situ chemical injections, or 
vapor extraction), Yankee evaluates its groundwater monitoring well network to confirm it 
is adequate to assess effectiveness.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-16.  If the existing wells are 
insufficient, Yankee installs additional monitoring wells.  Id.  When analytical results show 
contaminant levels below regulatory standards, the Company initiates quarterly 
compliance monitoring to account for seasonal fluctuations in groundwater level.  Id.  If 
contaminant concentrations fail to decline or rebound, Yankee performs additional 
subsurface investigations to determine if further remediation is required.  Id.  Yankee 
reported that no single monitoring timeline exists because site conditions, contaminant 
type, source accessibility, and plume size all influence monitoring periods.  Interrog. Resp. 
UPA-16. 
The Authority finds that Yankee’s environmental remediation activities primarily 
focus on legacy MGP sites, reflecting a risk management approach consistent with 
environmental stewardship expectations.  By integrating remediation efforts with 
municipal development plans and monitoring evolving regulatory requirements, Yankee 
demonstrates alignment with good principles of environmental risk mitigation and 
stakeholder engagement.  However, the Company’s reporting lacks operating 
company-specific metrics that clearly link remediation expenditures and site outcomes to 
long-term sustainability benefits or measurable risk reduction. 
Additionally, the absence of detailed performance indicators—such as quantified 
reductions in environmental liability, timelines for site closure, or progress toward 
sustainable redevelopment—limits transparency into how ratepayer-funded remediation 
contributes to broader goals, including community revitalization and equitable 
environmental outcomes.  While Yankee coordinates with municipalities and proactively 
monitors regulatory changes, there is limited evidence of systematic reporting that 
connects these actions to operating company accountability for ESG performance. 
As such, the Authority directs Yankee to develop and file, in its next rate case, 
remediation metrics, including:

community redevelopment integration;

These steps will improve accountability, align remediation activities with best 
practices, and ensure that expenditures deliver measurable environmental and 
community value while reducing long-term risk exposure. 
In response to Yankee’s Written Exceptions, while the Authority acknowledges that 
coordination with CT DOT and CT DEEP at certain sites reflects positive collaboration 
and municipal alignment, however such coordination does not, on its own, constitute 
evidence of structured ESG implementation or performance accountability at the 
operating company level.  Accordingly, there is no contradiction in the Authority’s findings: 
recognizing that remediation occurred and provided site-specific benefit is not equivalent 
to concluding that Yankee has demonstrated ESG transparency, stakeholder 
engagement, or outcome-based reporting. 
High enterprise-level ESG scores do not necessarily translate into meaningful, 
measurable ESG outcomes at Yankee itself.  The absence of clear ESG reporting at the 
operating company level prevents the Authority and stakeholders from evaluating whether 
Yankee’s remediation efforts deliver consistent, equitable, and transparent value to the 
communities that fund its operations.  As such, the Authority directs the Company to 
provide operating company-specific tracking of MGP site status, risk reduction progress, 
and community redevelopment coordination, as outlined above.

DEPRECIATION EXPENSES 
1. Summary 
A depreciation rate study proposes annual depreciation rates to be applied to plant-
in-service balances.  The product of the depreciation rate and corresponding plant 
balance is the annual depreciation expense, which is a charge to a company’s operating 
expense reflecting the annual recovery or amortization of previously expended capital 
investment.  While depreciation expense is a function of both the depreciation rate and 
the related plant balance, this section focuses only on the Authority's rationale for 
adopting OCC’s proposed depreciation rates.  The Authority’s determinations related to 
the Company’s plant balances are described in Section V.B, Plant-In-Service. 
Specifically, the Authority will consider: 
(1) Asset Categorization: To simplify the process, the utility categorizes its 
assets (or depreciable plant) based on common characteristics and 
expected service life.  Different asset categories (e.g., mains, services, 
equipment) will generally have unique depreciation rates to reflect the 
nature of the asset. 
(2) Service Life: The service life of each asset category is based on industry 
standards, historical data, and engineering assessments.  The service life 
is a key component to determining depreciation rates. 
(3) Net Salvage Value: The net salvage value is the gross salvage value of the 
asset less the cost to retire the asset.  In many cases, the net salvage value 
is negative.  The depreciation expense includes a portion of the net salvage 
value. 
(4) Method of depreciation: The most common method used is the straight-line 
depreciation, which spreads the cost of an asset evenly over its useful life. 
 
To determine the approved depreciation expense, the Authority utilized the Plant 
Model, which calculates depreciation expense by applying the corresponding

c. Net Salvage Rates 
When determining appropriate net salvage rates, it is important that the estimates 
reasonably reflect the Company’s actual experience with removal and salvage costs.  The 
depreciation study process necessarily involves judgment, but that judgment must be 
anchored in observed historical data to avoid over- or under-recovery.  Because net 
salvage represents a significant portion of total depreciation expense, even small 
deviations between proposed rates and actual experience can materially affect the 
revenue requirement.  For this reason, the Authority has closely examined whether 
Yankee’s proposed net salvage rates are consistent with the evidence in this proceeding. 
The Authority finds that Yankee’s proposed net salvage rates are excessive for 
several accounts.  Yankee refers to its approach as the “traditional method.”  See, e.g., 
Depreciation Panel PFT, p. 30.  Using the traditional method, net salvage estimates were 
computed from historical data on cost of removal and gross salvage, supplemented by 
the Company’s “statistical analyses and informed judgment” based upon “industry 
experience and the net salvage estimates for other gas utilities,” and expressed as a 
percentage of retirements.  Id., p. 25.  The computed net salvage estimates are then 
applied to assets in service to estimate future net salvage.  Id., p. 28.   
However, as OCC demonstrates, an analysis of Account 376 that relies only on 
historical data and omits the “statistical analyses and informed judgment” introduced by

Docket No. 24-12-01 
 
Page 160 
 
 
the Company in its traditional model produces an average net salvage cost of $1.36 
million over the preceding five years, or 1/11 of the nearly $15 million requested by the 
Company through its proposed annual depreciation accrual.  See generally OCC Brief, p. 
123; Dunkel PFT, pp. 7–11.  Instead of utilizing the traditional model, OCC’s expert 
proposes using the alternative historical cost method, which computes net salvage rates 
from recent, actual net salvage costs incurred by the Company.  Id., pp. 19–20.  Under 
the historical cost method, the Company would recover $4.1 million in net salvage, 
compared with the $1.36 million annual average actually incurred over the preceding five 
years and the $14.7 million proposed by the Company.  Id., p. 20. 
Mr. Allis’s rebuttal testimony makes three primary arguments opposing OCC’s 
position on net salvage methodology.  First, Mr. Allis claims that the historical cost method 
is “neither conceptually sound nor widely accepted in the industry.”  Allis Rebuttal Test., 
Apr. 11, 2025 (Depreciation Panel Rebuttal PFT), p. 24.  Second, Mr. Allis argues that the 
historical cost method is unsupported by the NARUC Public Utility Depreciation Practices 
(NARUC Manual).  Id., pp. 32–34, 40.  Third, Mr. Allis argues that the historical cost 
method results in inequitable cost recovery that may disproportionately shift net salvage 
costs to future customers.  Id., p. 56.  The Authority finds these arguments unpersuasive. 
First, although common practice in an industry can be a useful indicator of the 
reliability of a particular methodology, the Authority has a statutory mandate to, inter alia, 
ensure that public service companies perform their responsibilities with economy and 
efficiency and “that the level and structure of rates be sufficient, but no more than 
sufficient” to cover operating costs.  General Statutes § 16-19e(a).  Accordingly, the 
Authority declines to adopt an unduly deferential approach to current utilities practice in 
other states, particularly when such practice presents a substantial risk of over-recovery 
that far exceeds proven historical costs.  The Authority also maintains that undue 
deference to prevailing practices stifles innovation by prejudicing novel methodologies 
simply due to their novelty.  Finally, the Authority finds the historical cost method to be a 
reasonable way to estimate future net salvage rates due to its greater reliance on provable 
costs and reduced reliance on analytical judgment calls.  
Second, the Authority finds that the NARUC Manual is compatible with both OCC’s 
historical cost method and the Company’s traditional method.  Both methods utilize 
historical data to project future costs, differing primarily in the degree to which they rely 
on historical data as opposed to other analytical factors.  See, e.g., Depreciation Panel 
Rebuttal PFT, pp. 23–24 (“[B]oth Mr. Dunkel and I have used judgment that is based, in 
part, on the statistical analysis of historical net salvage data. . . .”).  The NARUC manual 
directly supports the use of historical data to estimate future net salvage.  See Dunkel 
PFT, p. 22 (quoting the NARUC Manual).  Additionally, although the Authority considers it 
neither dispositive nor binding, the Authority does not dispute that the traditional method 
is recognized by NARUC and utilized in other jurisdictions. 
Third, the Authority agrees with OCC that the record shows the traditional method 
results in inequitable cost recovery that disproportionately shifts future net salvage costs 
onto current customers.  See OCC Brief, p. 121.  Additionally, the Authority finds no 
evidence in the record proving that the historical cost method will prevent the Company

Docket No. 24-12-01 
 
Page 161 
 
 
from recovering all investment and removal costs, or that it will prove inequitable to current 
ratepayers.  To the contrary, the extreme disparity between the historical cost data and 
the Company’s proposed recovery under the traditional model raises substantial concerns 
about inequitable over-recovery from ratepayers, both present and future. 
Net salvage rates must take into consideration the totality of the evidence and 
circumstances presented in each case, with a net salvage method employed to arrive at 
just and reasonable rates.  Accordingly, the Authority adopts OCC’s interpretations of the 
record evidence and the historical cost method proposed by its expert witness.  In future 
proceedings, the Authority will continue to evaluate the reasonableness of proposed net 
salvage methods on a case-by-case basis to ensure systematic and rational cost recovery 
for the utility and fairness to customers.
