RATE DESIGN 
A. 
LEGAL STANDARD 
Yankee is a public service company within the meaning of General Statutes § 16-
1 and the Authority is statutorily charged with regulating the rates of Connecticut’s public 
service companies.  General Statutes § 16-19.  Consequently, Yankee must “file any 
proposed amendment of its existing rates with the [A]uthority.”  General Statutes § 16-
19(a).  Once a proposed amendment has been filed, the Authority:

Docket No. 24-12-01 
 
Page 171 
 
 
shall make such investigation of such proposed amendment of rates as is 
necessary to determine whether such rates conform to the principles and 
guidelines set forth in section 16-19e, or are unreasonably discriminatory or 
more or less than just, reasonable and adequate, or that the service 
furnished by such company is inadequate to or in excess of public necessity 
and convenience . . . . 
General Statutes § 16-19(a). 
Rate design objectives include: (1) the approval of cost-based, just, and 
reasonable rates that promote further equalization of rates across the Company’s 
divisions; and (2) revenue stability.  See General Statutes § 16-19e(a). 
In striking this balance and making pragmatic adjustments, the Authority is guided 
by General Statutes § 16-19e(a), which states, in relevant part, that the Authority shall 
examine proposed rates in accordance with the following principles: 
(4) that the level and structure of rates be sufficient, but no more than 
sufficient, to allow public service companies to cover their operating costs 
including, but not limited to, appropriate staffing levels, and capital costs, to 
attract needed capital and to maintain their financial integrity, and yet 
provide appropriate protection to the relevant public interests, both existing 
and foreseeable . . . (5) that the level and structure of rates charged 
customers shall reflect prudent and efficient management of the franchise 
operation. 
In furtherance of this statutory framework, the Authority typically employs the rule 
of cost causation, which allocates costs to customers and cost categories based on the 
costs they cause a utility to incur.  The Authority also generally attempts to equalize class 
rates of return, as that practice ensures that rates are not unreasonably discriminatory, 
while balancing the regulatory philosophy of gradualism to, among other things, avoid 
customer rate shock.  See J. Lazar et al., Electricity Regulation in the US: A Guide (2d 
Ed. 2016), p. 67, available at: https://www.raponline.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/rap-
lazar-electricity-regulation-US-june-2016.pdf (“sudden large rate changes should be 
avoided where possible to avoid undue new burdens on some classes of customers”).  
Consistent with the philosophy of gradualism, the Authority typically requires rate class 
revenue reductions or increases to be within one and one quarter times the overall 
distribution revenue increase.  See 16-06-04 Decision, p. 108; see also 13-01-19 
Decision, p. 153.  Finally, the Authority considers whether “existing or future rate 
structures place an undue burden upon those persons of [low-income] status” as 
contemplated by General Statutes § 16-19e(b).  The Authority weighs the above 
principles and considerations in determining appropriate cost and revenue allocation 
approaches and rate designs.

OCC is critical of Yankee’s zero intercept approach and results for the classification 
and cost allocation for Account 376 Mains.  OCC’s concerns include the small sample 
sizes, statistical insignificance of the intercept estimates, and lack of statistical analysis 
by the Company.  For example, when questioned about t-testing, the Company admitted

The zero-intercept method used by Yankee provides the estimated cost per foot of 
a hypothetical zero diameter pipe.  See Interrog. Resp. OCC-380, pp. 1, 3, 5, 6.  The 
intercept estimates produced by Yankee’s regression models were provided as part of the 
response to Interrogatory OCC-380, specifically pages 1, 3, 5, and 6.  The overall 
goodness of fit (“R-squared”) statistics and p-values for the diameter coefficients indicate 
confidence in the overall regression and diameter coefficient estimates as emphasized 
by Yankee.  However, the p-values and t-statistics for the intercept estimates suggest just 
the opposite and these intercept estimates are not reliable for the purposes of this 
approach.  Because the most important result for the zero-intercept approach are the 
intercept estimates as these provide the per unit cost of a hypothetical zero-diameter pipe,

analysis results, the Authority requires a reallocation of cost for FERC Account 376.

Currently, the Company benefits from several rate/revenue adjustment

1. Revenue Decoupling Mechanism 
a. Current Revenue Decoupling Mechanism 
The Authority first approved a RDM to decouple the Company’s distribution 
revenues from the volume of natural gas in the 18-05-10 Decision.  See 18-05-10 
Decision, p. 26; General Statutes § 16-19tt.  Under the approved RDM, the Company is 
authorized to perform an annual “true up” to reconcile actual revenues to revenues 
authorized in the Company’s previous rate case, collecting additional revenues as 
necessary to make up for any shortfalls in the previous year or conversely, crediting 
Yankee ratepayers if actual revenues exceed allowed revenues.  Id., p. 25.  In the 18-05-
10 Decision, the Authority ordered the Company to annually submit its RDM filing by 
March 1st of the subsequent calendar year.  Id., p. 38.  
Since 2020, the Company has annually filed an RDM for Authority approval.  The 
Authority last approved the Company’s 2024 RDM filing decoupling surcharge of 
$0.04243 per ccf to be charged to customers, effective April 1, 2025, through March 31, 
2026.  Motion No. 67 Ruling, Mar. 18, 2025, Docket No. 18-05-10. 
b. Approved RDM 
In any rate case initiated on or after October 23, 2023, the Authority has discretion 
in determining the decoupling mechanism and methodology used in a gas company’s 
decoupling order, subject to the principles set forth in General Statutes § 16-2(m).  
General Statutes § 16-19tt, as amended by Public Act 23-102.  In making such a 
determination, the Authority is required to consider factors, including, but not limited to: 
(1) whether the decoupling mechanism and methodology is in the best interest of 
ratepayers; (2) whether such mechanism and methodology adequately accounts for 
distribution system service outages; and (3) whether such mechanism and methodology 
adequately addresses the disincentive for utilities to engage in conservation and energy 
efficiency measures.  Id. 
The Company proposes maintaining a RDM.  The Company’s current RDM is 
based on a total revenue formula reflecting the base revenue authorized by PURA in the 
most recent rate case, in which PURA approved a three-year rate plan.  Rate Design 
Panel PFT, p. 14.  The Company proposes a formula in its MYPB rate plan that will 
determine the total revenue requirement to be used in the RDM each year, and the 
revenue target will be adjusted annually as prescribed by the MYPB rate plan in 
accordance with a performance based revenue adjustment formula (PBRA).  Id., pp. 14–
15.  Any over or under-recovery of revenue related to sales during a specific revenue 
decoupling period, when compared to the revenue target for that period, will remain as a 
separate line item on customer bills.  Id., p. 15.  The Company’s proposal includes special 
contract revenue, all distribution revenue, including other non-tariff-based revenue.  Id.

2. Distribution Integrity Management Program 
a. Overview 
In 2009, the United States Department of Transportation Pipeline and Hazardous 
Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) implemented integrity management regulations 
for natural gas distribution systems, or DIMP regulations, that are intended to help ensure 
pipeline integrity and improve pipeline safety.  See 49 C.F.R. Part 192, Subpart P.  The 
DIMP regulations require pipeline operators to analyze their pipeline systems, 
circumstances, and programs to identify potential weaknesses that could result in high 
consequence accidents and to address those weaknesses before accidents occur.  Id.  
The DIMP regulations became effective February 2, 2010, and required gas companies 
to have a plan, i.e., a DIMP, implemented by August 2, 2011.  49 CFR § 192.1005.  The 
Authority, through the Gas Pipeline Safety Unit (GPSU), has been involved with this 
rulemaking since its inception.  GPSU worked with the NGA and the Connecticut gas 
companies to ensure proper implementation of what is considered the largest set of new 
regulations affecting distribution companies since the Natural Gas Pipeline Safety Act of 
1968.  See 10-12-02 Decision, p. 171.

Docket No. 24-12-01 
 
Page 184 
 
 
The DIMP regulations promulgated by PHMSA are set as a baseline minimum 
safety level for the entire country.  See 49 C.F.R. Part 192, Subpart P.  Due to the 
significant variances between gas companies, their infrastructure, and their respective 
geographic regions, the DIMP regulations are mostly performance based in nature.  The 
DIMP regulations do not specifically state that the replacement of cast iron or bare steel 
pipe is required.  Id.  The regulations instead state that gas companies must: have 
knowledge of the systems; identify threats to the systems; evaluate and rank the risks; 
identify and implement measures to address the risks; measure performance; monitor 
and report results; evaluate effectiveness; and periodically evaluate and improve the 
program.  See 10-12-02 Decision, p. 171. 
One of the key elements of DIMP is the need to show improvement in the safety 
of the company’s system.  Id., p. 172.  Cast iron and bare steel piping are considered 
threats to safety because of leaks that are caused by several factors, including cracking 
of cast iron and corrosion of bare steel.  Id. 
The company has identified existing bare steel and cast-iron mains as two of the 
leading threats on its distribution system.  Application, YGS-CAPITAL-1 (Capital Additions 
Panel PFT), p. 77.  The company seeks to reduce this risk through its ARP.  Copper 
services, coupled steel, and unprotected steel were added to the ARP in the company’s 
last rate case, since these facilities were also identified as high threats to the system.  
See Docket No. 18-05-10; Capital Additions Panel PFT, p. 77.  The company uses a risk 
assessment model called the “Gas Asset Management Evaluation System” (GAMES) to 
prioritize gas mains for replacement; the model uses leak history, pressure systems, 
location of main, and corrosion leaks as inputs.  Capital Additions Panel PFT, p. 12. 
The Company tracks leak rates over time to evaluate the effectiveness of its 
ARP.  Data from 2009-2023 shows a reduction in leaks occurring on cast-iron and bare 
steel mains.  Id., p. 56, Fig. 2.  Overall leak rates (for all pipe types) are also tracked and 
generally show a downward trend from 2014 to 2023.  Id., p. 59, Fig. 5. 
The Authority ordered the Company in the last rate case to spend the amount 
necessary to replace leak prone infrastructure by specific target dates.  18-05-10 
Decision, p. 38 (Order No. 10).  For example, Order No. 10 required that cast iron and 
bare steel facilities be fully replaced within 11 years, while unprotected coated steel mains 
and services were to be replaced within 14 years, following a risk-based system 
replacement methodology.  Id.

c. Authority Analysis 
The DIMP program and associated DIMP Reconciliation Mechanism have some 
similarities to the water companies’ Water Infrastructure and Conservation Adjustment 
(WICA) program.  Both programs address mains that require replacement by allowing for 
a rate mechanism that provides advance cost recovery outside of a rate case.  However, 
in terms of cost recovery, the WICA program differs from the gas DIMP program in that 
the WICA program is statutorily authorized, and has cost recovery thresholds in place that 
limit (on a retail revenue percentage basis) the amount that a water company can request 
under the WICA program between rate cases.150  Although Order No. 8 of the 18-05-10 
Decision requires the Company to annually file a reconciliation of the difference between 
the DIMP revenue requirement in base distribution rates and its actual DIMP 
expenditures, the current DIMP program has no cost recovery measures in place that cap 
such expenditures.  18-05-10 Decision, p. 26.  From a rates perspective, this could lead 
to years where annual DIMP expenditures will increase dramatically going forward. 
The Authority recognizes that the ongoing mains replacement program is essential 
to maintain public safety and network reliability.  For these reasons, the Authority will 
continue the DIMP program.  However, because there are no cost recovery thresholds in 
place, the Authority is concerned that under the current DIMP rate mechanism, the DIMP 
reconciliation has and will likely continue to experience revenue deficiencies, after the 
rate year expires.  The Authority reviewed OCC’s proposal regarding the DIMP rate 
mechanism and determines that certain elements of OCC’s proposal provide solutions 
that may alleviate the Authority’s concerns regarding the existing DIMP rate mechanism, 
including annual filing requirements that clearly explain the planned DIMP activities and 
budgets.  Larkin-Connolly PFT, p. 48.   
The Authority finds OCC’s proposal to disallow expanding the DIMP Reconciliation 
Mechanism to include investments ($17,493,000) for complying with new safety 
regulations reasonable and appropriate as the Company’s proposal lacks specifics.  
Additionally, the Authority supports establishing an annual cap on cost recovery through 
the DIMP Reconciliation Mechanism as a cap will create more certainty and eliminate 
volatility in addition to providing clear expectations concerning budgetary issues in the 
annual DIMP rate mechanism reconciliation.  The Authority finds that a rate cap proposal 
is a balanced and reasoned approach that protects the interest of the ratepayers while 
continuing to support pipeline system safety.  The Authority recognizes that while miles 
completed is a valid measurement of DIMP program progress, other factors such as 
greater risk of failure, population served, and municipality concerns must be considered 
in measuring progress and public safety.  To ensure the DIMP program runs efficiently,

5. Earnings Sharing Mechanism 
An ESM is a ratemaking mechanism that shares a utility’s earnings in excess of its 
allowed ROE between the utility’s ratepayers and its shareholders.  The Authority 
established an ESM for Yankee in the 10-12-02 Decision.  10-12-02 Decision, p. 138.  
Under the Company’s approved ESM, the Company is required to split any earnings 
above its allowed ROE in any calendar year equally between the gas company’s 
ratepayers and shareholders, i.e., 50% to ratepayers and 50% to shareholders.  Id. 
The Company shall continue its ESM with a 50/50 split from the first dollar of over-
earnings above the allowed ROE.  See 23-11-02 CNG Decision, p. 187; 23-11-02 SCG 
Decision, p. 204.  Additionally, the Authority directs the Company to calculate the ROE 
using the lesser of the: (a) authorized debt and equity capitalization; or (b) the actual 
carried equity position, and to apply ESM carrying costs as of January 1 of the subsequent 
year.  In addition, the Company is directed to separately identify and exclude all 
disallowed costs from its most recent rate case from ESM reporting on a going forward 
basis, and to provide an affirmation of the accuracy of its disallowed expenses.  Going 
forward, the Authority will approve the Company’s annual ESM filings, subject to a full 
prudency review in the Company’s next rate case.  This guidance will allow the Company 
to achieve its authorized ROE based on its authorized capital structure while ensuring 
that the Company shares excess earnings with ratepayers in accordance with the rate 
case decision.  This approach will also ensure that customers are not negatively impacted 
in situations where the Company incurs expenses related to projects, programs, or other 
items not approved in directives or orders outlined in this Decision.

The Hurdle Rate Calculation Methodology is a financial model used by the gas 
companies to determine whether the expected revenue contribution from a new customer 
is sufficient to meet the minimum required LDC-specific rate of return on capital 
investments that is necessary to connect the customer to the system.  If the new 
customer’s contribution is less than the underlying connection costs, the customer must 
provide a contribution in aid of construction payment to recover the shortfall.  The length 
of the payback period in the Hurdle Rate Calculation Methodology determines whether 
the new customer or the gas company’s ratepayers pay more of the costs required to 
connect the new customer to the system.

b. Authority Analysis 
Based on the Authority’s development of the electric LIDR, gas LIDR for CNG and 
SCG, and the evidence presented in this docket, the Authority adopts the Company’s 
proposal to develop a five-tier LIDR structure that uses the tier income eligibility guidelines 
as proposed, adopts a 2% annual billed revenue budgetary target, and includes a usage 
cap.  As EOE suggested, the Company shall develop the usage cap capability such that 
the usage cap level can be adjusted as needed.  Such design elements align with 
approved modifications to the electric LIDR structure.  See 17-12-03RE11 2024 Decision.   
However, the Authority finds it appropriate to limit the Company’s LIDR offering to 
customers to only one 10% discount at this time.  The Authority agrees with OCC and 
EOE that there is a lack of record evidence as well as opportunities for stakeholder 
engagement to determine the appropriate discount levels for each tier.  Further, CNG and 
SCG are currently updating their billing systems to create a five-tier LIDR structure but

However, based on Yankee’s testimony that there would be a significant incremental cost

ratepayer funds to establish a tiered LIDR now, which can then be adjusted at a later date

to have all gas customers experience the same LIDR offering (i.e., a 10% discount) while 
each company develops the capacity for a five-tier LIDR design structure for prudent and 
efficient future LIDR modifications.   
Accordingly, the Authority directs the Company to design and build the capacity for

a 10% discount level for each tier, only launching one tier with a 10% discount level, etc.).

exploring the remaining gas LIDR design elements.

first was given the opportunity to…address the issue and then [it] objectively made an 
error” and one which must be escalated to EOE.  Hr’g Tr., May 29, 2025, 278:22-25; 
279:1–4; 284:8–20; Hr’g Tr., June 6, 2025, 1613:7-9 (“These are just the, the complaints 
that come through EOE through our formal resolution process that we have established 
with EOE.”).  The Company also considers a “justified complaint” as something different 
than an imperfect call.  Hr’g Tr., 278:22–25; 279:1-4.   
Instead of referring to them as complaints, Yankee states that customers submit 
“inquiries.”  See Late Filed Ex. 11; Hr’g Tr., 1606:19 (“So if it’s their first outreach, it would 
not be a complaint.”).  Yankee does not consider a complaint justified until “the customer 
has first contacted Eversource and given the Company a chance to address their issue; 
AND the Company has objectively made an error.” Late Filed Ex. 16.  As OCC sums up, 
“Yankee applies a standard where the only justified complaint is one in which the 
customer contacted Yankee; Yankee erred in its response; the customer subsequently 
contacted EOE; and EOE contacted Yankee.” EOE Brief, p. 161

EOE highlighted examples of complaints where customers had reason to complain 
and valid complaints but where these complaints were not treated as “justified complaints” 
by the Company because the complainants did not contact EOE.  Late Filed Ex. 16.  
Looking at data from years 2018-2024, even when complainants went to EOE, only 58 of 
the 1,094 complaints which came through EOE to Yankee were considered “justified 
complaints.”  Interrog. Resp. EOE-21.  OCC raised the well heeded point that “Customer 
service is not limited to simply being given the first opportunity to fix a mistake.  The best 
customer service should strive not to make the mistake at all.”  OCC Brief, p. 162. 
The Authority agrees that more discussion is needed on this topic.  There is a 
disconnect between how the term complaint is used in common parlance and how the 
Company uses the term complaint.  If metrics are to be beneficial, they must track 
meaningful data.  At this stage, the Authority is not confident that the data being tracked 
under Yankee’s definition of “justified complaint” will provide data which accurately 
represents the type and number of communications which come from customers who are 
dissatisfied with some aspect of the Company’s approach.  The Authority will consider 
setting up a working group or technical meetings on this metric approach so that 
interested parties can have the opportunity to provide comments and recommendations.   
Similar to the PBR metrics discussed in Section III, Multi-Year, Performance-Based 
Rate Plan, the Authority finds that the current proceeding is not the appropriate forum to 
investigate, develop, and adopt this metric.  This proceeding lacks coordination with the 
other gas companies in Connecticut and sufficient stakeholder process.  Coordination on 
customer service metrics between gas companies in Connecticut would best benefit 
customers so that all are held to the same standards and practices. 
XII. 
ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL, AND GOVERNANCE PRACTICES 
A. 
OVERVIEW 
The Authority finds that although Yankee is included in Eversource’s overall energy 
planning, it does not have its own ESG or GHG goals, performance targets, or defined 
responsibilities.  ESG and GHG planning are conducted at the enterprise level, and 
Yankee is not assigned a specific role in achieving those goals.  While this centralized 
structure may offer consistency across Eversource, it limits visibility into how Yankee 
contributes to broader environmental and social outcomes.  Further, the information 
offered to by Yankee as to Eversource’s practices was vague and limited.   
Yankee does not maintain its own GHG or ESG goals.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-1.  
Instead, Eversource adopts GHG and ESG goals at the enterprise-wide level and does 
not assign them to individual operating companies.  Id. Yankee also lacks standalone 
employee culture and engagement goals.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-10.  Moreover, 
Eversource did not assign Yankee a pro-rata share of responsibility for achieving 
enterprise-level GHG or ESG objectives.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-2.   
Eversource claims it tracks certain GHG and ESG objectives targets at both the 
State and operating company levels.  Id.  Yankee’s long-term planning was incorporated 
into Eversource’s enterprise-level integrated energy strategy, which addressed the future

gas and electric needs of customers.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-38.  This integration aligned 
Yankee’s planning efforts with Eversource’s broader GHG and ESG goals, particularly in 
areas not governed by specific regulatory mandates.  Id. 
This lack of complete operating company-level accountability makes it difficult for 
the Authority to assess whether Yankee’s operations support the State’s clean energy 
goals or other policy objectives.  It also prevents stakeholders from understanding what 
ESG progress is being made within the utility’s local operations.  To improve transparency, 
Yankee shall provide clear documentation of how Yankee’s activities contribute to 
Eversource’s enterprise-wide goals.  Given that Yankee admits that its ESG initiatives 
“are generally managed and funded through normal business practices,” the Company 
should accordingly include performance tracking at the operating company level.  
Interrog. Resp. UPA-4.  Accordingly, the Company shall file operating company-specific 
ESG targets and performance data in its next rate amendment application. 
B. 
ESG INITIATIVES 
The Authority finds that the Company’s current approach to ESG implementation 
lacks clarity at the operating company-level.  By embedding ESG-related activities—such 
as safety, environmental compliance, and training—within general business operations 
and funding them through base distribution rates, the Company does not clearly 
distinguish these efforts from its routine obligations.  As a result, it is difficult to determine 
which ESG-related actions are being taken at Yankee, how they are prioritized, or whether 
they reflect broader enterprise goals or Connecticut-specific needs. 
Within Eversource, ESG initiatives—such as climate resiliency, environmental 
compliance, employee safety and training, and ethical conduct—are not managed as 
standalone programs.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-4.  Instead, these activities are integrated into 
the Company’s day-to-day operations.  Id.  For Yankee, that means that the Company 
considers these functions embedded within routine business practices rather than 
organized under any distinct ESG framework.  Id.  With the exception of regulatory 
mandates like the Accelerated Replacement Program, which included ESG-related 
benefits such as emissions reductions and safety improvements, it does not appear that 
ESG initiatives are treated as separate efforts.  Id.  As a result, ESG initiatives were 
funded through base distribution rates as included in broader operational budgets.  
Interrog. Resp. UPA-4. 
In addition, Eversource stated that ESG practices—as well as efforts related to 
employee culture and engagement—were conducted at the enterprise level, not through 
individual operating companies.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-5.  The Company referred to its 
annual Sustainability Report for a broader overview of enterprise-level ESG efforts.  Id.  
Eversource considers advancing ESG leadership and fostering a strong organizational 
culture remained key components of its overall business strategy and customer service 
model.  Id.  As a result, Yankee does not maintain its own ESG or employee engagement 
initiatives, and claims no activities of this kind were funded specifically by Yankee 
ratepayers.  Id.

For performance tracking, Eversource monitored performance against its GHG

While the use of internal scorecards and governance structures may support

into ESG activities at the operating company-level, stakeholders are left without a clear 
understanding of how stated commitments translate into action within Connecticut and 
benefits to Connecticut ratepayers. 
The Authority directs the Company to identify and report ESG activities at the

otherwise expected to benefit Connecticut customers.  Clearer documentation of these

C. 
GHG AND REDUCTION EFFORTS 
The Authority finds that Yankee lacks operating company-specific GHG emission 
goals and relies entirely on Eversource’s enterprise-wide carbon neutrality strategy.  
While the enterprise approach provides general alignment and leverages corporate 
resources, it does not offer transparency into Yankee’s direct contribution to emission 
reductions or how its operations uniquely support statewide climate priorities.  This lack 
of operating company accountability is further underscored by the limited availability of 
Yankee-specific data beyond fugitive methane leaks, which hinders the ability to assess 
localized emission trends, or the effectiveness of mitigation measures funded by 
Connecticut ratepayers. 
The Authority finds that Yankee’s primary emission reduction effort, the 
Accelerated Replacement Program (ARP), has delivered measurable benefits by 
reducing methane emissions from leak-prone pipes, with progress tracked through 
internal dashboards and planning tools.  However, these internal tools are not reflected 
in public reporting and are not linked to operating company-specific benchmarks or 
interim reduction targets.  Without such transparency, stakeholders cannot evaluate 
whether Yankee’s infrastructure investments are meeting expectations for emission 
reduction performance or how these outcomes align with customer costs and 
environmental risk mitigation. 
Eversource does not assign Yankee specific GHG emissions goals, apart from 
those associated with regulatory requirements such as leak-prone pipe replacement 
under the ARP.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-11.  Instead, Eversource managed its GHG efforts 
at the enterprise level, preparing an annual GHG inventory for all operating companies 
combined and aligning emission reduction strategies through a dedicated ESG and

Climate Governance structure.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-38; UPA-52.  The enterprise-wide 
carbon neutrality goal by 2030 covered Scope 1 emissions (e.g., fuel use at facilities, fleet 
emissions, Sulfur Hexafluoride, switchgear, and methane emissions from gas networks) 
and Scope 2 emissions (electricity usage at facilities and line losses) but excluded indirect 
Scope 3 emissions such as customer natural gas consumption.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-52. 
Yankee contributed to these enterprise-wide goals primarily through ARP, which 
replaced aging, leak-prone pipes with modern materials to reduce methane emissions.  
Interrog. Resp. UPA-15.  GHG reductions from Yankee’s ARP were factored into the 
broader Eversource carbon neutrality strategy, particularly regarding methane emissions 
reported as part of the operational footprint.  Hr’g Tr., 568:9–23.  To monitor progress, 
Yankee used internal ARP planning tools and dashboards to track expected and actual 
emission reductions associated with these infrastructure upgrades.  Id., 569:2–9.  While 
Eversource published corporate GHG inventories in its Sustainability Reports, data at the 
operating company level is limited due to legacy data systems and shared assets.  
Interrog. Resp. UPA-51.  Currently, the only Yankee-specific data included in the 
enterprise GHG inventory related to fugitive methane leaks from mains, services, and 
distribution equipment.  Id.  Eversource is developing systems to allow for more granular 
tracking by operating company in the future.  Id. 
For verifying emission reductions, Eversource stated that all GHG data underwent 
third-party review and that incremental improvements to data gathering and calculation 
methodologies are incorporated into each annual update.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-12.  The 
Company indicated that, although permitting and community approval challenges 
occurred in some municipalities, these issues did not materially delay ARP progress or 
the associated reductions in GHG emissions.  Id. 
The Authority directs Yankee to include in its next rate amendment application, 
operating company-specific reporting on GHG reduction efforts, including ARP progress, 
interim methane reduction results, and any additional emission-related initiatives that 
support the corporate carbon neutrality goal.  This reporting shall identify gaps in data 
availability, provide actions to enhance operating company-level GHG tracking, and 
demonstrate how these efforts deliver measurable benefits to Connecticut customers who 
fund Yankee’s operations.

Yankee was asked to clarify how ESG goals were weighted relative to other 
performance factors in executive compensation and what impact missing ESG targets 
would have if financial or operational goals were met.  Hr’g Tr., 555:6–12.  Yankee 
explained that ESG sustainability goals were included within the Eversource’s overall 
funding metric, which allocates 70% to financial measures and 30% to operational 
measures.  Hr’g Tr., 554:13–16.  The Company stated that because sustainability goals 
represented a portion of the 30% operational component, it was mathematically possible 
for overall funding to remain available, even if sustainability targets were missed, provided 
strong financial performance was achieved.  Id., 555:16–20.  Executives with direct 
accountability for sustainability or ESG goals in their departments were evaluated within 
a zero to 200% payout range determined by their manager.  Id., 555:21–25.  The 
Company added that executives with ESG-related goals had those metrics more heavily 
weighted in their individual performance evaluations compared to executives whose roles 
do not include ESG responsibilities.  Id., 556:1–8.  No specific percentage within the 30% 
operational portion was assigned to ESG goals; instead, weighting was determined at the 
manager’s discretion, resulting in heavier evaluations for executives with ESG 
responsibilities than for those without such responsibilities.  Id., 556:11–22.  Executive 
compensation goals are re-evaluated annually as part of the Company’s performance 
management process.  Id., 559:1–3.  Goals were set by senior leadership and cascaded 
throughout the organization, becoming more tactical at lower levels, while 
leadership-level goals remain strategic or developmental in nature.  Id., 558:11–20.  ESG 
and sustainability goals were often multiyear objectives, requiring evaluation of interim 
performance against long-term outcomes.  Id., 559: 4–6.  Yankee’s ESG compensation 
metrics, historically based on peer-relative ESG ratings, had recently been expanded to 
include internal key performance indicators addressing departmental sustainability 
priorities.  Id., 559:11–25. 
The Authority finds that Eversource’s ESG compensation structure is applied at 
the enterprise level, limiting visibility and influence at the operating company level.  ESG 
weightings for executives are determined largely by managerial discretion, without fixed 
percentages, and are not linked to Connecticut-specific or Yankee-specific outcomes.  
This lack of structured alignment makes it difficult to determine whether ESG 
performance—particularly in areas tied to environmental justice, GHG emissions, or local 
stakeholder engagement—translates into tangible, ratepayer-facing results.

The Authority clarifies that it is not directing the Company to alter its internal 
compensation structure.  Rather, it recommends that the Company assess whether 
greater transparency and accountability could be achieved by incorporating operating 
company-level ESG metrics into future compensation plans, particularly for executives 
whose roles directly impact Connecticut operations.  Such metrics, if implemented, would 
help demonstrate alignment between executive performance incentives and the State’s 
sustainability and equity policy goals. 
As such, the Authority recommends that the Company consider whether 
department-level or operating-company ESG metrics tied to measurable environmental 
and social outcomes should be incorporated into future compensation plans, including 
whether fixed weightings are warranted to ensure consistent alignment with measurable 
sustainability and equity objectives.  Absent these enhancements, the Authority lacks a 
clear evidentiary basis to determine whether ESG-linked compensation produces 
meaningful value for Connecticut ratepayers.

through Yankee-specific programs.  Hr’g Tr., 575:9–20. 
The Authority finds that Yankee’s workplace diversity and inclusion efforts lack 
clearly defined operating company-specific structure and accountability.  Although 
Eversource administers enterprise-wide DE&I programs and reports workforce 
composition data, these efforts are not anchored to Yankee-specific goals or benchmarks.  
As a result, there is limited visibility into diversity and inclusion outcomes within Yankee’s 
workforce.  Furthermore, the absence of direct participation in certain external leadership 
development programs and the reliance on corporate-level strategies, rather than 
Yankee-specific initiatives, further diminishes transparency and prevents measurable 
progress.  Yankee’s collaboration with union leadership, while supportive of fair and 
transparent processes, does not incorporate specific diversity-related provisions or

measurable operating company-level goals to evaluate whether these efforts

The Authority further finds that Yankee does not link its broad recruitment

representation and advancement gaps within its workforce.  This lack of focused 
accountability prevents stakeholders from understanding whether Yankee’s workforce 
reflects the communities it serves or whether development opportunities are equitably 
available across all employee groups.  Such transparency is particularly important 
because a workforce that mirrors its customer base and provides equitable advancement 
pathways supports customer trust, strengthens service quality, and fosters inclusive 
decision-making that benefits ratepayers. 
As such, the Authority directs Yankee to present, in its next rate amendment

outcomes.  These DE&I goals need not constitute quotas or hiring targets based on

and improve workforce inclusion consistent with applicable law.  The Company shall also 
include data on employee participation in external development programs and internal 
advancement efforts, and any identified gaps in representation or promotion, along with 
actions taken or planned to address those gaps.  Moreover, developing Yankee-specific 
metrics and reporting structures will enhance transparency and demonstrate whether 
DE&I efforts produce equitable workforce outcomes aligned with the communities Yankee 
serves and the customers who fund its operations.  This is particularly relevant given the 
$37,000 in human resources and training costs allocated to Yankee ratepayers, 
underscoring the need for clarity on whether these expenditures directly support 
measurable workforce inclusion and development outcomes. 
4. ESG and DE&I Training 
Eversource stated that it does not provide standalone ESG training because its 
sustainability initiatives and priorities are integrated into various company practices, 
including environmental stewardship, compliance, health and safety, and corporate 
ethics.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-49, p. 1.  ESG-related concepts are incorporated into 
functional trainings which are offered across different job roles.  Id. 
In addition to general ESG content, Eversource implemented two enterprise-wide 
equity-focused training modules.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-36-RV01, p. 2.  The first, Equity 
Fundamentals, launched in 2022 with a target of training 50% of employees by year-end 
2023.  The Company exceeded its goal, with 100% of employees completing the training.  
Id.  In 2024, Eversource launched a second module, Equity in Action, designed to provide 
continuous learning on environmental justice issues through scenarios and stories that 
demonstrate how employees embed equity principles into daily work and 
decision-making.  Id.  This training also exceeded its 65% participation goal, with 100% 
employee completion.  Id.

Separately, Eversource offers two ongoing training programs focused on 
workplace inclusion: Creating an Inclusive Workplace and Inclusive Leadership.  Interrog. 
Resp. UPA-49, p. 1.  The Creating an Inclusive Workplace is a self-paced eLearning 
course available to all employees on demand, while the Inclusive Leadership is a live, 
voluntary training for supervisors and above.  Id.  The Inclusive Leadership course was 
conducted on multiple dates throughout 2024, including March 5, March 21, April 2, April 
18, May 7, May 23, June 4, September 10, September 19, October 1, October 17, October 
31, November 5, and November 21, 2024, with no sessions scheduled for 2025.  Id., p. 
2. 
The Company explained that these programs focus on building inclusive 
leadership skills, addressing bias and micro-messages, and equipping employees with 
strategies to foster belonging and engagement across teams.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-49, p. 
2.  These trainings are voluntary and designed to promote continuous education, 
leadership skills, and inclusive workplace culture.  Id.   
Additionally, Credit and Collections customer service representatives receive 
quarterly customer engagement training designed to recognize and address bias when 
interacting with customers regarding arrearages or past due balances, ensuring 
respectful and equitable service.  Interrog. Resp. UPA-50. 
The Authority finds that while Eversource provides employee culture and inclusion 
training opportunities, these programs are implemented enterprise-wide and are not 
specific to Yankee.  As a result, there is limited transparency into how training initiatives 
directly influence Yankee’s workforce or address operating company-level equity 
priorities.  Additionally, the voluntary nature of most training offerings, such as Inclusive 
Leadership and Creating an Inclusive Workplace, limits assurance that all employees, 
particularly those in leadership positions, consistently receive diversity and inclusion 
training. 
The Authority also observes that while Eversource exceeded its internal 
participation goals for equity training, Yankee does not track outcomes that demonstrate 
whether these programs translate into measurable changes in workplace culture, 
representation, or advancement opportunities.  This gap prevents stakeholders from 
evaluating whether ratepayer-funded allocations, such as leadership development or 
training costs, are producing tangible and equitable workforce outcomes for Yankee 
employees. 
As such, the Authority directs Yankee to report in its next rate amendment 
application, operating company-specific DE&I training objectives, participation tracking, 
and where possible, measurable outcomes demonstrating the effectiveness of such 
programs in advancing diversity, equity, and inclusion across its workforce.   
G. 
FUTURE POTENTIAL ROE REDUCTION 
Yankee’s continued reliance on enterprise-wide ESG, DE&I, and environmental 
remediation initiative—without developing operating company-specific goals, metrics, or 
accountability structures—creates a significant transparency gap for Connecticut

Docket No. 24-12-01 
 
Page 215 
 
 
stakeholders.  While Eversource promotes its ESG leadership, top-quartile external 
ratings, and numerous national accolades, these achievements do not demonstrate 
measurable value or outcomes at the Yankee level.  Ratepayers fund portions of these 
activities, yet there is no clear line of sight into how the expenditures translate into local 
environmental benefits, workforce diversity improvements, or equitable service 
outcomes.  The absence of Yankee-specific reporting prevents the Authority, 
stakeholders, and the public from evaluating whether the Company’s professed ESG 
commitments produce tangible results in the communities it serves. 
This lack of specificity is particularly concerning given the Company’s consistent 
messaging that ESG principles are integral to its long-term strategy and corporate culture.  
If Eversource can integrate ESG into executive compensation, corporate branding, and 
investor relations, it should likewise be able to integrate measurable ESG accountability 
into Yankee’s operations.  The failure to track and report on concrete local outcomes, 
such as improvements in workforce representation, measurable environmental risk 
reduction, or direct community benefits undermines the credibility of these corporate 
claims.  In effect, Eversource leverages the reputational and financial advantages of ESG 
accolades while providing little evidence that these benefits extend to the customers who 
fund its operations. 
Accordingly, the Authority clarifies that it is not imposing an immediate adjustment 
to the authorized ROE in this proceeding.  However, the Authority finds that the continued 
absence of meaningful, operating-company-specific ESG action, performance metrics, 
and value creation could warrant consideration of a downward ROE adjustment in a future 
rate case, based on the record evidence at that time.  Any such adjustment would follow 
a full prudence review and be supported by clear findings consistent with Connecticut law.  
The Authority emphasizes that this forward-looking determination is intended to 
encourage measurable progress and alignment between enterprise-level ESG 
commitments and local accountability—not to serve as a penalty.  To maintain credibility 
and demonstrate commitment to Connecticut-specific outcomes, Yankee must provide 
clear evidence in future filings that its ESG and DE&I programs deliver quantifiable 
benefits to Connecticut ratepayers and align with the State’s environmental and equity 
priorities.
